#5736. Novel ADC Boosts Survival in Pretreated Endometrial Cancer

— Sac-TMT is currently under review at the FDA for a post-platinum/immunotherapy indication

Results from the TroFuse-005 trial presented at the annual European Society for Medical Oncology congress showed that the investigational antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) sacituzumab tirumotecan (sac-TMT) significantly improved progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival compared with physician's choice of chemotherapy in patients with advanced or recurrent endometrial cancer who had previously been treated with platinum-based chemotherapy and immunotherapy.

In this exclusive MedPage Today video, investigator Domenica Lorusso, MD, PhD, of Humanitas University in Italy, discusses the phase III findings, which are currently under review with the FDA.

Following is a transcript of her remarks:

In TroFuse-005, we did compare sac-TMT versus treatment of physician's choice (between doxorubicin or weekly paclitaxel) in advanced or recurrent endometrial cancer patients [previously] exposed to platinum [chemotherapy] and an immune checkpoint inhibitor, given separately or in combination. The trial had a dual primary endpoint, [PFS] and overall survival -- [PFS] evaluated by blinded independent central review -- and secondary endpoints were overall response rate, duration of response, and quality of life.

The trial met both the primary endpoints. A statistically significant and clinically relevant 41% reduction in the risk of progression was reported in patients treated with sac-TMT, with a median PFS increasing from 3.9 to 7.2 months.

But also a statistically significant and clinically relevant reduction in the risk of death was reported in patients treated with sac-TMT -- the hazard ratio was 0.68, so a 32% reduction in the risk of death, with a median overall survival increasing from 12 to 19 months.

And a significant increase in overall response rate was reported, with overall response rate doubling in patients treated with sac-TMT -- overall response rate was 17% versus 35% -- with a median duration of response of 6.9 months in the standard arm versus 11.1 months in the experimental arm.

This is the most important aspect. This did not impact the quality of life of the patient. From baseline to the pre-specified week 12, there was no difference between quality-of-life scores [between] treatment groups.

So, for all these reasons -- increased [survival] advantage, manageable toxicity profile, no impact in quality of life -- we really believe that this drug should be considered the new standard of care in this population and the new control arm in the next generation of clinical trials.

#5735. Australian Plugin Vehicle Market Steady in October — Update

… with a spotlight on the Great Wall Motor ORA 5 rising star.

CleanTechnica readers were probably hoping for the surge to keep surging Down Under. I was. However, it appears to have remained steady. Not the flash in the pan petrolheads were hoping for at least. In September 2026, 108,778 passenger vehicles were sold, including all drivetrains. See the charts here.

Battery electric vehicles (BEVs) achieved a market share of 24.2% (26,287 units), outselling petrol-only and diesel-only vehicles. Add in 10,072 plugin hybrid (PHEV) sales and you get a plugin penetration rate of approximately 34%. PHEV sales are the fastest growing segment in Australia — increasing 122% year on year. For those who care, 17,843 HEVs sold in October (a YoY increase of 20%). I am looking forward to peak HEV, followed by peak PHEV, as we have seen in more mature Scandinavian markets.

Australia’s EV penetration rate (including BEV and PHEV) has hovered in the low to mid 30% for the last few months. Not sure what the future holds, but even just maintaining this rate for a few months will make a difference. Nothing beats lived experience. My neighbours are now asking about how much it costs to fill up. One came for coffee yesterday and stayed to go for a drive in our new Model Y. He was very impressed with the tech, the finish, and above all the running costs. He confided that he had just filled up his wife’s Honda Civic — AU$82 — and his Isuzu D Max — AU$121.

On a recent shopping expedition, we counted 10 electric cars in the car park, out of 50 vehicles. Not just Tesla and BYD, but also Zeekr, Geely, the GWM ORA 5, and a Deepal. Battery electric vehicles are making their presence felt. But not all my friends can see them. They can spot Tesla and BYD vehicles, but they tell me they don’t see any other EVs on the road. Yes, we have tried to educate them, but it is not working just yet. “See if it has an exhaust pipe. Does it have a sealed front?”

One car that I am seeing in ever increasing numbers is the refreshed Great Wall Motors ORA — now in an SUV body and a much cheaper price. When it launched back in 2023, I expected great things (see our review here). Sadly, the Funky Cat (as it is known in China) did not live up to expectations. It was the cheapest EV in Australia at the time (AU$46,000) but couldn’t compete with the BYD Dolphin and the MG 4. Now, relaunched as an SUV and with a more appropriate price (AU$34,000 — scratch that, just got an email that knocks another grand off the price), I am seeing them everywhere — 6 on the highway just yesterday.

So, on to the best-selling BEVs on the Australian market in October 2026:

Pretty much the same as last month. Obviously, BYD was the best-selling brand, closely followed by Tesla. BYD has six cars among the top twenty BEVs. There are no cars from Korean, Japanese, or European carmakers in the top ten BEV numbers. When all powertrains are considered, BYD is the second highest selling brand behind Toyota in the Australian market. There seems to be some talk in the auto news about Tesla and BYD being considered “legacy” brands — who would have thought?

Expect big things from Geely as it aggressively expands throughout Australia. Geely recently announced that it has opened 100 dealerships over the past 18 months. Its EX5 sales figures are putting pressure on the competition in the medium-SUV-segment Mazda CX-5, Hyundai Tucson, Mitsubishi Outlander, and Nissan X-Trail.

Utes still dominate the Australian market. When a compelling BEV offering becomes available, the top ten may change again. I was excited to see the KGM Musso BEV ute, but it has failed to gain traction. Only 269 have sold in the past few months. The Toyota BEV Hilux only has 14 units in the country — likely to be demonstrators. PHEV utes seem to be doing much better, led by the BYD Shark. Over 15,000 have sold so far this year.

Now for some newsy titbits: Dealers for established brands are calling for a temporary ban on new car brands (read Chinese made cars) entering Australia, as they cannot compete. The boss of the Australian Automotive Dealer Association says the industry has reached a crisis point, with the last quarter delivering the first loss since the global financial crisis. Chinese brands now own 36% of new car sales.

“This is a clear warning that the commercial settings underpinning our industry are becoming unsustainable,” Mr Voortman said. He speculates on the possible risks to consumers: “… the influx of new brands also puts consumers at risk, as it can lead to rapid depreciation of vehicles, a lag in parts supply, longer repair times, and orphaned vehicles should those companies choose to leave the country.”

Though, what we are seeing in Australia is that legacy brands, mainly European, are the ones leaving the country.

#5734. Australia's Cheapest New Car Is This $13,000 MG Hatchback, And It's Far From A Stripper

Chinese cars have been beating down on long established performance and luxury car brands for a while now, all while costing a fraction of the price. From jumping over potholes to setting top speed records to beating Land Cruisers in off-road tests and even having emergency water travel capabilities, there are some mighty impressive pieces of kit across the Chinese car industry. What I'm most interested in, though, are the ultra-cheap economy cars that sell for the price of a used shitbox, and that's exactly what the MG3 offers to Australian car buyers. It's a compact hatchback with the face of a plecostomus, which isn't especially exciting, but its $13,020 USD price sure is.

It's no stripper, either. That bargain price includes features like Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, steering wheel controls, air conditioning, a digital driver's display, an auto-hold function, automatic power window switches, and adaptive cruise control with lane centering. It even has a standard feature that the new Toyota RAV4 doesn't even offer on its most expensive trim level that happens to be four times the price of the MG3: padded front and rear armrests. OK, so the MG3's actual MSRP in Australia is $13,890.85 USD at current exchange rates, but the fact that a dealer was even willing to discount it further is remarkable, too.

As you can see from CarSauce's review, the MG3 is woefully slow. Its 1.5-liter four-cylinder engine sends just 109 horsepower and 105 pound-feet of torque to the front wheels via a continuously variable transmission, which results in a leisurely 0-to-62 mph time of 12.57 seconds. It ain't quick, but it gets the job done, and again, it's a $13,000 car. The last car sold in the United States that was near the $13,000 mark was the diminutive Chevrolet Spark, which ran the 0-to-60 sprint in 10.8 seconds in Car and Driver's testing, so the MG3 isn't too far off that pace. Plus, looking beyond straight-line speed (or lack thereof), the reviewer even says it rides great and handles respectably, which are not always the case with bargain-basement cars.

Sadly the MG3's weak engine doesn't equate to exceptional fuel efficiency, with the presenter's real-world economy equating to about 36 mpg on the highway and more like 26 mpg around town. Those aren't abysmal numbers, just perhaps not as good as one might hope from such a weak engine in a tiny car.

Beyond the lower-than-low base price, the MG3's value proposition really comes into focus when you take into account its 10-year manufacturer warranty. For those who say, "why spend $13,000 on the cheapest new car available when you can buy a bigger, better used car for the same price?" Consider the idea of spending $13,000 on a car with a 10-year-long warranty versus spending that same amount on a used car with no warranty. The new car comes with an entire decade of mechanical coverage so the buyer doesn't have to worry about unexpected repair costs for those 10 years, whereas the used car could end up requiring costly repairs within the first year of ownership.

There are some quality concerns noted in the video, including infotainment software glitches and some apparent inconsistencies in the operation of those fancy automatic windows, but considering the price and that stellar warranty, I'd say the pros outweigh the cons in this case. For those who view their cars as another appliance, or those who simply want the financial security of not worrying about repair costs for a whole decade, the MG3 must be a pretty tempting option. Provided you live in Australia, of course — or Mexico, Europe, the Middle East, or other parts of the world where it's pretty damn cheap, too.

#5733. New Medicare Payment Model for Back Pain, Heart Failure Riles Docs

— Physicians will face payment cuts for subpar performance in treating those conditions

Physician groups are seeking a delay for a new Medicare demonstration model debuting January 1 that mandates doctors who treat low back pain and congestive heart failure (CHF) patients meet performance standards or face payment cuts.

The Ambulatory Specialty Model (ASM) will affect doctors who treat as few as 20 patients with back pain or 20 patients with heart failure. Those physicians will automatically be placed in the model, which will apply to specialists in any of 235 geographic areas nationwide that have been selected for the 5-year demonstration program.

According to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), the model is aimed at addressing the fragmented care that chronic disease patients often receive. "ASM will promote preventive care and more effective upstream chronic disease management by rewarding ASM participants ... for improving patient health outcomes and coordinating with primary care providers," the agency said on its website. "Successful outcomes include reducing avoidable hospitalizations and unnecessary procedures, improving patient experience, and lowering costs to Original Medicare."

Under the model, "ASM participants will receive a positive, neutral, or negative payment adjustment on future Medicare Part B claims for covered professional services," which includes any service covered by Medicare for any Medicare patient -- not just patients with low back pain or CHF -- according to CMS, with payment adjustments ranging from -9% to +9% in the first 2 ASM years, increasing to -12% to +12% by the final year.

An individual doctor's payment increase or decrease would depend on how well that doctor performed on a set of outcome measures compared with their peers, rather than being measured against a pre-set standard benchmark -- an approach known as a tournament model.

Physician groups have several concerns. "As proposed, the model guarantees that most participating physicians will see their payments cut no matter how well they perform on the measures," John Whyte, MD, MPH, CEO and executive vice president of the American Medical Association (AMA), wrote in a comment letter to CMS when the model was proposed last year.

Instead of achieving Medicare savings by reducing physician payment rates, the AMA urges CMS to help physicians in reducing avoidable Medicare spending on hospitalizations and other services, the letter stated. The AMA also suggested the model should be voluntary and that "CMS should also set a performance standard in advance instead of using a 'tournament' approach."

Physician practices that have already begun preparing for model implementation are running into problems, according to a joint letter sent on Oct. 27 to CMS Deputy Administrator Abe Sutton, JD, and signed by the AMA as well as the American Hospital Association, the American Medical Group Association, the Medical Group Management Association, and the National Association of Accountable Care Organizations, among others.

"These delays and setbacks include, but are not limited to: delayed receipt of the final participant list; delayed access to the ASM portal; challenges with logging into, accessing, or delegating authority within the portal; and receiving timely help and guidance from ASM subject matter experts," the letter said. In addition, the final ASM participant list wasn't published until Sept. 15, about 2 months later than CMS originally said it would be, leaving participants only 3 months to prepare.

Due to these and other difficulties, "the undersigned strongly urge [CMS] to delay ASM's launch until all operational and technical infrastructure is available, tested, and ready for the model to start," the letter said. "If [the agency] maintains the January 1, 2027, start date, participants should not be subject to downside financial risk for the initial performance period while operational infrastructure stabilizes."

That immediate downside risk is new for a CMS demonstration model, according to Jennifer Hananoki, JD, senior counsel at the Holland & Knight law firm in Washington, D.C.

"The risk there is no on-ramp here," Hananoki said in an online interview. "A lot of times, when CMMI [the Center for Medicare & Medicaid Innovation] is putting in place new models, especially models in areas where there hasn't been an alternative payment model in the past, they'll have a ramp-up period --  a period of upside-only risk" where practices get paid more for doing well but don't suffer penalties if they perform worse than average. "But that doesn't exist here. The risk [of penalties] really starts almost immediately."

The lack of a firm benchmark is also a problem, she added. "They need to see the benchmark in advance. They need to see how they would have performed in the past in order to understand -- 'Hey, for some reason my costs are below the median or above the median, and I need to figure out why because I need to continue that trend forward, or I need to make adjustments.' And so, there's concern that some of these really fundamental aspects of what makes for successful alternative payment models, all those ingredients might not be there yet."

Another way the ASM isn't like other Medicare physician payment models -- such as the Merit-Based Incentive Payment System, or MIPS -- is that it is meant to be money-saving rather than budget neutral, said Harold Miller, president and CEO of the Center for Healthcare Quality and Payment Reform in Pittsburgh, and the author of a report on the ASM.

"This is not budget neutral," he said in a phone interview, explaining that CMS is taking a 15% cut of the money saved with physician penalties, instead of putting all of that money into bonuses for higher-performing physicians, as MIPS does. Basically, CMS is saying, "'For every $100 we'll take away, [physicians] will get $85 back,'" he said.

There's also a concern that more doctors could be added to the participant list over time, said Jeffrey Davis, a senior policy advisor at Holland & Knight, in an online interview. "They did release a participant list the first year with 5,500 folks," said Davis. "But they could add more depending on if they want to expand the geographical regions or even, you know, [add] the new physicians that come into that region."

Rather than delay the program, CMS should abandon it entirely, Miller suggested. "It doesn't solve a problem. If we're stuck with it, don't make it mandatory," he said, "and have a predefined performance score. That would make this a less bad program."

#5732. A Tribute to Bunker Roy: The Man Who Turned Village Grandmothers into Solar Engineers

Sanjit “Bunker” Roy, who taught illiterate grandmothers to become solar engineers, passed away peacefully this morning at his home in Tilonia, Rajasthan, aged 81.[1] I first encountered his work not in India, but in the rain forests of Borneo.

It was October 2016, and as night fell, the surrounding Borneo tropical rain forest had come alive with noise, dominated by the trill of frogs and the rhythmic pulse of cicadas. I was about to embark on the Sabah study tour of the Emerging Leaders Dialogue Asia (ELDA). Over the next two weeks, we would visit timber plantations, mountain communities recovering from a deadly earthquake, and marine parks.

But undoubtedly the highlight for me was discovering the inspiring story of Barefoot College, which trains village grandmothers to be solar engineers. On our first evening, while enjoying a mini feast of banana fritters, pomelo, and langsat (a bit like lychees but more delicious), we were told about the college’s remarkable partnership with the Sabah Women Entrepreneurs and Professionals Association (SWEPA) in Borneo.

Barefoot College was the brainchild of Bunker Roy, and he was an unlikely revolutionary. Born into privilege in Bengal in 1945, he was educated at the Doon School and St Stephen’s College, Delhi—two of India’s most elite institutions—and was a national squash champion. A conventional career beckoned. Then, during the Bihar famine of the mid-1960s, he saw rural poverty firsthand, and his life changed course.[2] When he told his mother he wanted to live and work in a village, he later joked, she “went into a coma” and didn’t speak to him for a long time.[3]

In 1972, Roy settled in Tilonia, a dusty village in Rajasthan, and founded the Social Work and Research Centre (SWRC), which later became known as Barefoot College. Its rules turned conventional education on its head. Anyone with a university degree was disqualified from studying there, and no degrees were awarded. In 2011, Roy said that nobody at the college earned more than $100 a month. The campus itself was built in 1986 by a dozen local “barefoot architects” who could not read or write, and it went on to win an Aga Khan Award for Architecture. At the college’s night schools, children aged 6 to 14 elect their own prime minister and cabinet.[4]

Roy’s guiding conviction was simple: “There is no urban solution to a rural problem.”[5] He was awarded the Padma Shri, one of India’s highest civilian honors, in 1986, and named one of Time magazine’s 100 most influential people in 2010.[6] He is survived by his wife, Aruna Roy, the former civil servant who led the grassroots movement behind India’s Right to Information Act.[7]

The positive impact of his work has been immense. By the college’s own count at its 50th anniversary in 2022, it had trained 1,708 illiterate and semi-literate rural women from 96 countries as solar engineers, bringing light to more than a million people in over 75,000 households and saving about 45 million liters of kerosene. Its rainwater harvesting had captured some 70 billion liters and brought safe drinking water to more than 1,650 schools. More than 90,000 working children had studied in its night schools, and its barefoot health workers had treated over 300,000 patients.[8]

During our study tour, SWEPA arranged for us to meet one of Barefoot College’s beneficiaries, a so-called solar mama. She was part of the program that takes illiterate grandmothers from poor rural villages and, within six months, trains them at the college in India for their new job. They return to their villages to install and maintain full solar lighting systems. Roy deliberately chose grandmothers because they are rooted in their communities; men and younger people, he found, were more likely to take their new skills and leave for the city.[9] Because the women shared no common language, much of the training was done through sign language and hands-on practice.[10]

Malaysia’s first solar mama—very likely the woman I met that evening—was Tarihing Masanim, from Kampung Sonsogon Magandai, near Kota Marudu in Sabah. She completed her training in India in 2015 and returned to bring electricity to around 100 homes in her village.[11] Roy loved to tell stories like hers. One of his favorites was about a 55-year-old Afghan grandmother who electrified 200 houses and set an Afghan engineering department head straight on the difference between AC and DC.[12]

The story of the solar mamas captures many elements of what it means to harness the power of responsibility to create a more inclusive society and economy. So many barriers are being broken through, as these amazing women challenge stereotypes about age, gender, and rural capacity. Barefoot College shows that sustainable development—including adopting sustainable technologies—is an option for people living with low incomes in remote villages. The Barefoot model empowers people to be agents of their own destiny.

Bunker Roy stands out as an inspiring example of inclusive leadership. His impact, which is so strongly evidenced by the solar engineers program, is as much about restoring dignity to those who are traditionally excluded as it is about developing or transferring practical skills. Roy, who said he had “a very elitist, snobbish, expensive education in India” that “almost destroyed” him, explained:

“So we started the Barefoot College, and we redefined professionalism. Who is a professional? A professional is someone who has a combination of competence, confidence and belief. A water diviner is a professional. A traditional midwife is a professional. A traditional bone setter is a professional. These are professionals all over the world. You find them in any inaccessible village around the world. And we thought that these people should come into the mainstream and show that the knowledge and skills that they have is universal.”[13]

Roy ended that talk with a line often attributed to Mahatma Gandhi, whose principles guided his life’s work: “First they ignore you, then they laugh at you, then they fight you, and then you win.”[14] For the solar mamas of Barefoot College, and for the more than a million people whose homes they have lit, Bunker Roy won.

This article draws from content in Wayne Visser’s book Thriving: The Breakthrough Movement to Regenerate Nature, Society, and the Economy (New York: Fast Company Press). For more information, see waynevisser.com.

#5731. Tesla 'Full Self-Driving' One Step Closer To Recreating Human Driving By Overtaking Bicycles, Exceeding Speed Limits And Misidentifying Road Signs

Humans are imperfect, so at least in theory, robotaxis are supposed to save us by doing all the perfect driving we aren't able to do. Of course, had we poured every dollar that's been spent on robotaxi development into improving public transportation, self-driving cars would feel unnecessary. But the bigger problem is, after all those billions of dollars and years of development, Momentum Mag reports that a recent test of Tesla's so-called "Full Self-Driving" software found that it loved to speed through neighborhoods, illegally pass cyclists, and break other traffic laws. So basically, it drives like your least-favorite neighbor.

Woke 3 already killed the Cybertruck, so Tesla's school bus-passing software could be next on the chopping block after liberals figure out how to make every man a little shorter every time he disappoints a woman. Until then, it's important to know how good or bad the software controlling some of the most popular new cars actually is, which is why Belgian mobility organization johanna.be put the software to the test and found it frequently breaks speed limit laws in areas where drivers are most likely to hit pedestrians or cyclists. So that's not great.

Additionally, while there aren't many places in the U.S. where drivers can't legally pass a cyclist, that isn't the case in Belgium. You'd think fine-tuning the software to account for changes in laws between countries would have been a pretty basic part of Tesla's development, but nope. In johanna.be's testing, it found that Tesla's FSD system "repeatedly tries to overtake cyclists in cycle streets, something that is explicitly illegal in Belgium."

Coincidentally, right around the time johanna.be published the results of its Tesla safety test, the European Transport Safety Council shared the results of a separate safety test. The ETSC found that Tesla's "speed offset" and "contextual max speed" features don't follow United Nations or European Union rules regarding safety, and it's called on member states to reject both features later this year when the EU plans to hold an important vote on advanced driver assistance system regulation.

The ECF is also asking the EU to create a European Road Safety Agency that would act as "an independent EU body able to investigate issues involving automated systems and share the subsequent findings with other Member States." Even before the ETSC got involved, johanna.be's findings were concerning enough to warrant some serious attention from international regulators that Elon Musk wasn't able to gut. As the ECF put it, Tesla's so-called "Full Self-Driving" software (emphasis is the ECF's):

If a human loved to drive at 150% of the posted speed limit, regularly told people the speed limit was higher than it was, and kept trying to make illegal passes, we'd take their license and tell them to take the bus. With robotaxis and cars with driver-assist systems, it should be the same. Until they can prove they actually follow the rules of the road, there's no reason to let them on our roads. We also shouldn't allow automakers to sell driver-assistance systems that haven't been proven safe, either. Even if you disagree, I don't think you need a PhD in traffic safety to understand the argument there.

That said, it's entirely possible that safety researchers are criticizing Tesla for mistakes that every automaker's software makes. The problem with that argument is that johanna.be ran the same test with a Citroën C3 that managed to correctly identify all seven speed limit signs. For comparison, the Tesla got six of the seven speed limits wrong. It only got one correct. Imagine not only being wrong, but being more wrong than the French. Self-immolation is probably the only option.

While we wait to see how the EU's member states vote, the ECF also noted that otherwise docile behavior is no excuse for Tesla's software behaving badly in other ways. As it noted:

the study also found that FSD behaved cautiously and courteously around pedestrians and cyclists in general, yielding early, giving space, and even slowing for a sleepy cat in the road! However, this should not compensate for a pattern of speeding and illegal overtaking in streets that are primarily designed for safe walking and cycling

#5730. CAR-T Therapy: Mixed Results in Rheumatoid Arthritis Trial

— Six patients treated: three show strong responses, three not so much

ORLANDO -- Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) may not be as amenable to chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy as has been the case in lupus and certain other autoimmune conditions, research presented here suggested.

Among six patients with very refractory RA treated in the first part of a phase I/II trial called COMPARE, three achieved low disease activity within 6 months after a single infusion of CAR T cells, and no severe adverse reactions were seen, according to David Simon, MD, of Charité University Hospital in Berlin, speaking at the American College of Rheumatology annual meeting.

That was the good news. The not-so-good was that the other three did not achieve low disease activity by standard criteria, and one of those who did experienced a disease flare during the final months of the yearlong study.

This was a more "heterogeneous" response pattern than has been seen with CAR-T therapies in lupus, Simon said. It may not be all that surprising, however, because RA itself is heterogeneous (not all patients develop autoantibodies, for example) and the role of B cells -- CAR-T therapy's main target -- is not as prominent as in lupus and some other autoimmune disorders.

One reason for trying this approach has been that the anti-B-cell drug rituximab (Rituxan) has been helpful in difficult RA cases. That suggests that, at least for some patients, B cells do help drive RA and that the "immune reset" concept with CAR-T treatment, which aims to wipe out B cells' autoimmune memory, could work effectively in RA.

Indeed, these initial results indicate that it's a realistic proposition -- it's just that the pathology differs enough between patients that the efficacy will be uneven.

The phase I portion of COMPARE recruited patients with heavily pretreated RA. Simon said the six who were enrolled had previously tried a mean of 6.5 targeted therapies, in addition to conventional drugs such as methotrexate, without achieving adequate disease control. Disease Activity Score values across 28 joints (DAS28) ranged from 4.6 to 6.8 among the six patients, who were in their early 30s to late 60s. Disease duration spanned 4.5 to 24 years. Three were women and three were men.

As a phase I study, safety was a top priority to examine. Simon said all patients experienced cytokine release syndrome, which is nearly universal with CAR T-cell therapy in oncologic as well as rheumatologic use. None, however, developed more severe reactions such as immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS) or a condition called LICATS (local immune effector cell-associated toxicity syndrome) that resembles ICANS but affects other organ systems besides the nervous system. As well, no infections more severe than grade 2 occurred; the only adverse effect rated as serious was elevated liver enzymes in one patient.

All patients showed deep depletion of B cells, as expected, almost immediately after CAR T-cell infusions. But other effects were more variable. Four of the six patients showed abolition of autoantibodies, and as noted above, only three achieved DAS28 scores below 2.8, the threshold for low disease activity; none got to zero, whereas full remission has been common with CAR-T therapy in lupus.

Simon spent several minutes discussing the patient who flared. This was a 42-year-old woman with a DAS28 score of 5.5 at baseline. Crucially, and unlike the other five patients, analysis of CAR T-cell counts in circulation showed very poor expansion in the first weeks after the infusion -- short of 100 cells per μL at the maximum, compared with approximately 150-400 cells per μL in the others. B-cell reconstitution was already well underway at week 8, whereas it was week 16 for the next earliest, and still later for others. Analysis of reconstituted B cells indicated that autoreactivity had not been abolished, thus paving the way for relapse that began sometime after week 36.

"Whether the observed immune remodeling translates into durable drug-free disease control remains uncertain," Simon concluded. "Follow-up is limited to approximately 1 year, and re-emergence of autoreactive B-cell populations in one relapsing patient suggests that immune reconstitution may influence long-term outcomes."

Ten more patients will be recruited for COMPARE's phase II portion, which, as the name suggests, will include a control group treated with rituximab.

#5729. Polestar Formula 2030 Concept Makes Us Hope Polestar Will Be Back In America By 2030

Chinese-owned Polestar was banned from selling cars in the U.S. back in June, and like a scorned ex showing you what you're missing after a breakup, it's now revealed one of the coolest designs in recent memory: the Formula 2030 concept car. Look at what they took from us.

It's got a low, wide, shooting brake shape. The big front door, little rear door setup is pure enthusiast bait, and the switchgear inside looks like it came straight off of professional audio equipment. The Formula 2030 isn't just a for-show concept car, either, because Polestar says it will indeed "point towards future design direction for the brand."

Specifically, "various design attributes" seen here will actually show up in the next-gen Polestar 2 and upcoming Polestar 7 compact SUV. The Formula 2030 is billed as a compact four-door sports car, not really fitting neatly into any existing segment. It sits lower than the Polestar 5 grand tourer, fits between the 2 compact sedan and 7 size-wise, and is probably closest to the Polestar 4 in spirit.

It already looks great at a glance, but things get way more interesting once you start opening stuff up. Both the hood and rear hatch open up clamshell-style, exposing the natural fiber composite chassis underneath and orange Öhlins dampers. The half-size rear doors are coach doors, giving the Formula no B-pillar and a huge opening when all doors are open.

Inside, a very curved instrument screen measuring 20 inches sits on top of the steering column while a 12.2-inch center touchscreen sits in the middle. That touchscreen can physically lower when the driver switches drive modes to Performance, and raise when the car is in Autonomous. Below this screen is an array of up to eight customizable rocker switches and knobs. You can swap the specific switches or knobs out, like you can with, say, a pro-grade video game controller, and their individual functions can also be configured to your liking. All four bucket seats sit low in the cabin and get inflatable bolsters and cushions for better support.

I've never really thought about how rare four-spoke wheels are, but looking at the 22s on this Polestar concept, I'm simultaneously sad that they aren't more common but also completely understand why that's the case. They're definitely weird, but I also sort of dig it?

It all adds up to a funky yet beautiful design that makes us hope Polestar will return to the U.S. market by the Formula 2030's namesake. Given the political conditions that led to its banning and how those tides are turning in this country, that scenario actually feels like a real possibility.

#5728. Oh, So That’s Who’s Buying All Those New Subaru Trailseeker EVs…

After EV sales in the US crashed into a brick wall last year, the Subaru Trailseeker has been one of the few points of light. Newly introduced this year, Trailseeker has racked up a relatively decent sales track record in the crowded SUV field. As for whether or not Subaru can continue to grow its EV sales in the US, the automaker’s elaborate, multi-faceted “Subaru Loves Pets” campaign has emerged as the secret weapon…

The Subaru Loves Pets campaign first appeared 18 years ago, back in 2008. A lot of demographic and cultural water has passed under the bridge since then. More so than in past generations, pets have taken on the role of family members equal to, if not superior to, anyone else in the household. And if that’s the case, shouldn’t pets have their own seatbelts, too?

Now Subaru’s longtime relationship with the pet-centered population is beginning to muscle into EV territory. One indication of a connection between pet and EV preferences surfaced in October, when Subaru released a new report indicating that pets wield a noticeable influence on purchasing  preferences in the US auto market overall.

Commissioned from the firm Talker Research, the report is based on interviews with 2,000 and pet owners in the US. Of that cohort, a resounding majority of 73% said they are more likely to drive for the holidays, specifically in order to travel with their pet.

“As the holidays approach, more than two-thirds (68%) said their pet will affect their travel plans this year, and nearly half (45%) have turned down travel opportunities that couldn’t accommodate their pet,” Subaru adds.

Households with pets also have distinct priorities for a vehicle. “Plenty of room between pets, passengers, and luggage tops the list of features pet owners say matter when traveling with an animal,” Suburu reports.

“More than one in four (26%) prioritize cargo space for crates, carriers, beds, or gear. Among hybrid and EV drivers, that climbs to 35%,” the automaker further notes.

If you missed the money quote, it’s that thing about 35% of hybrid and EV drivers prioritizing space for pet gear, compared to just 26% of drivers overall. In addition to the traveling-with-pets angle, that generational difference also reflects a sharp generational divergence in attitudes towards EVs.

“Electric vehicles have become a political flashpoint in Washington. But new national polling finds the biggest divide among potential EV buyers isn’t political. It’s generational,” reports the advocacy organization ZETA (the Zero Emission Transportation Association) in September.

“Seventy-five percent of adults ages 18–34 and 72% of adults ages 35–49 say they are likely to purchase or lease a new EV within the next five years,” ZETA elaborates. “Among adults ages 50–64, that number falls to 50%. Among those 65 and older, it drops to just 23%, a striking 52-point gap between the youngest and oldest Americans.”

Now let’s take another look at the Subaru survey. Talker Research found that 75% of Gen Z and 70% of millennials traveled with a pet within the past five years, compared with just 58% of Gen X and only 40% of baby boomers (looking at you, Mitt Romney).

A similar generational difference surfaced in other areas of the survey:

Younger pet owners are also more likely to say they plan travel around their pet, with 42% of Gen Z and millennials doing so compared with 27% of Gen X and boomers.

Among pet owners who haven’t yet road-tripped with their pet, 74% of Gen Z and millennials would consider it, compared with 54% of Gen X and boomers.

Subaru pulled back on its overall electrification plan for the US market after last year’s EV sales crash, but it did follow through on the new Trailseeker, offered for sale on a limited basis in January of this year. Volume deliveries to dealers began in April of this year, and in May the Trailseeker racked up 1,074 in sales. The number is vanishingly small compared to industry leader Tesla but a promising start in the challenging US market. By August, Trailseeker had a total of almost 5,000 in sales for the year to its credit, rising to 6,006 sold by the end of October.

All else being equal, recognition from Wards Auto may help keep the momentum going. On October 13, Subaru announced that the Trailseeker earned a slot in the 2026 Wards 10 Best Engines & Propulsion Systems list.

“For 2026, Wards evaluated 26 powertrains from returning winners as well as all-new or significantly updated cars, trucks, or SUVs. They were evaluated on several criteria, including power, torque, refinement, efficiency, and innovation,” Subaru notes.

“Its 375 horsepower combined with immediate electric powertrain response always satisfies. Its range estimates also hold up well in real-world driving, interstate and all. Yet Subaru keeps the price completely reasonable given such capability,” said Robin Warner, who manages the 10 Best Engines & Propulsion Systems program.

By “completely reasonable,” Warner means the Trailseeker’s starting MSRP of $39,995 and its estimated range of 281 miles. According to Subaru, the Trailseeker can go from 10% to 80% charged in as little as 28 minutes, with up to 150 kW on a DC-fast charger.

“With an onboard battery preconditioning system, enabled either by navigating to a charging destination or by the driver via touchscreen controls, the Trailseeker can charge its battery in cold climates — as low as 14 degrees Fahrenheit — at speeds comparable to those in normal weather conditions,” Subaru also advises.

In addition to the seal of approval from Wards, on October 29 Subaru announced that Trailseeker earned the “Car of the Year” award in the 2027 TopGear.com US Car Awards program

The automaker cites Top Gear US Correspondent Alex Kalogiannis, who was particularly enthused about the vehicle’s off-road performance. ““Off the beaten path, the set-and-forget X-MODE figures out all the tricky terrain stuff as you trundle through the bush, and with about 8.5 inches of ground clearance, it can scale all but the scariest obstacles in your path,” Kalogiannis remarked, somwhat colorfully.

“People still carry a torch for the WRX and its many rally-inspired incarnations, but the heart of Subaru fandom now is its dutiful, rugged, useful wagon – the Trailseeker,” he added.

That remains to be seen. Trailseeker will have to compete for the hearts and minds of Subaru fans against other models in the automaker’s lineup, including gasmobiles. The SUV-styled Outback wagon, for example, clocked 118,470 in sales from January to the end of October this year, and that was not the only Subaru model to hit six figures.

Still, US President Donald Trump has provided Subaru and other automakers with a new opportunity grow their EV sales profile this year. On February 28 the President launched his war against Iran, sending global oil prices on an upwards trajectory and improving the affordability case for EVs regardless of the loss of the $7,500 federal EV tax credit, which Trump and his Republican majority in Congress axed last fall.

Ever since dropping the first bombs on Iran, Trump has repeatedly claimed that the war is over, or almost over, or over any minute. In the latest pronouncement, on  Monday Trump said that multilateral negotiations over a peace settlement in Iran are in a state of “positive momentum toward an end.” And if you believe that…

#5727. Michèle Mouton Driving A Quattro S1 Up Pikes Peak Is The Coolest Way To Promote Audi's New Q7

The first thing that comes to mind when you mention Quattro is probably Audi's 1980 Group B rally car. It makes perfect sense that the German manufacturer would lean on that legacy when promoting its new Q7 and SQ7 SUVs that have the trademarked all-wheel-drive system, but the company did something much cooler for its new ad campaign: Audi reunited Michèle Mouton with a Quattro S1 at the iconic Pikes Peak hill climb. The 1982 World Rally Championship runner-up still looked at home behind the wheel of the 493-horsepower rally monster.

Audi's new ad campaign titled "Performance Runs in the Family" features a pair of videos: a typical 30-second TV spot, and a 4-minute short with Mouton driving a Quattro S1 up Pikes Peak. During the visually stunning drive up the Colorado mountain, she reminisced about the animosity she faced during the 1985 hill climb, her winning run, and how the ascent has changed in the 41 years since.

Mouton was the first woman and the first non-American to win the Pikes Peak International Hill Climb. The Frenchwoman set a record time of 11:25.390 up the treacherous 12.4-mile ascent, besting the previous record set by Al Unser Jr. in 1983 by 13 seconds. Mouton is still effortlessly cool, still delivering pointed one-liners as naturally as the rest of us breathe. During the revival run, she noted, "When I was at this spot in the race, I had no time for feelings."

The 30-second TV spot mixes archival footage of Mouton during the Group B era with footage of a 2027 Audi SQ7 driving up Pikes Peak. To emphasize the campaign's legacy theme, the ad features Mouton alongside her daughter, Jessica. The third-generation Q7 isn't as nimble on the twisting mountain roads as a Group B rally car, but that isn't the point. The SUV's new styling looks just as aggressive and far more comfortable for a family. Vito Paladino, Audi of America's President, stated in a release:

"Audi's story of quattro didn't end with rally racing. That connection between performance and everyday capability is what makes quattro such a defining part of our brand. The all-new Audi Q7 family carries that legacy forward, bringing together Audi's performance heritage with the innovation and engineering that define the next generation of our vehicles."

The 1985 Pikes Peak International Hill Climb was Mouton's last event with Audi before she departed for her farewell season with Peugeot. The Frenchwoman and her accomplishments will forever be tied to Audi. Mouton's four WRC victories with the Audi Quattro are a legacy every four-wheel-drive model produced by the German automaker inherits. It's not merely laurels to rest on, but a level of performance that Audi has to honor.

#5726. Nanobody Shows Promise in Myasthenia Gravis

— PREVAIL trial found rapid improvement with a once-weekly subcutaneous injection

Results from the phase III PREVAIL trial presented at the American Association of Neuromuscular & Electrodiagnostic Medicine annual meeting showed that treatment with the investigational once-weekly nanobody gefurulimab significantly improved symptoms in adults with anti-acetylcholine receptor antibody-positive generalized myasthenia gravis, with a safety profile generally comparable to placebo.

In this exclusive MedPage Today video, James Winkley, MD, of Baptist Health Medical Group in Lexington, Kentucky, discusses the findings, including the potential convenience of self-administered treatment with the subcutaneous injectable and compatibility with intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) therapy.

Following is a transcript of his remarks:

The PREVAIL study was a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial with gefurulimab as the treating agent. Gefurulimab is a unique agent in that it's the first nanobody that'll be used in myasthenia gravis, which makes it a smaller molecule, which allows for greater tissue penetration and solubility -- so it can be given as a [subcutaneous] injection rather than the larger monoclonal antibodies, which have to be given in larger volumes underneath the skin or as IV infusion. So this would represent a greater ease of access for patients to have a [subcutaneous], once-a-week injection that doesn't require them to go to the infusion center.

As we had seen in the trial, similar to eculizumab [Bkemv] and ravulizumab [Ultomiris], which are C5 inhibitors, it met its primary outcome of MG-ADL [Myasthenia Gravis Activities of Daily Living] reduction, with a minus 4.2 reduction versus 2.1 on placebo, which was statistically significant. We did see a quick onset of action within 1 week, with a statistically significant reduction in the MG-ADL for those patients, as well as 4 weeks for the [Quantitative Myasthenia Gravis].

There were similar side effects between the treatment group and the placebo group, with injection-site reactions being slightly higher in the treatment group, but all of those reactions tended to be mild to moderate. The most common adverse events were headaches, upper respiratory infections, and muscle aches and pains. One thing that was significant at any time we're using complement inhibitors, there were no meningococcal infections. Everybody made sure they were fully vaccinated, and if they'd had to be started prior to 2 weeks, they received antibiotics. But we had a very typical safety profile, as I said, between the placebo arm and the treatment arm -- the side effects were similar.

This is going to make for ease of access for patients. You still have other molecules out on the market. You've got a once-daily complement inhibitor and you've got now a once-every-2-weeks IV infusion versus every 8 weeks. So kind of depending on what the patient prefers, this gives them greater access. We've got an easily portable complement inhibitor that patients no longer are tethered to an infusion center that they have to worry about. When's our next infusion? Do I have access? And I think that's going to be a huge advantage for the patients and their quality of life.

I would say that one thing that's unique about [gefurulimab] is that it is compatible with IVIG. And so the other larger monoclonal antibodies like the FcRn [neonatal Fc receptor] and the larger eculizumab and ravulizumab, it gets recycled by a different mechanism because it goes through the albumin on the FcRn receptor. It was combined with IVIG during the trial, patients could be on stable dosages of it, so it has that advantage of being able to be compared and not have to give supplemental dosing.

So I think that it will have combination with other available medications. I think that's a big advantage for it.

#5725. Norway’s Electric Snowplow Worked. Sweden Added Hydrogen Anyway.

Norway has already demonstrated battery-electric snowplowing on one of its toughest mountain highways. A Scania 45 R covered roughly 7,000 km on Hardangervidda, plowing, grading and spreading sand through a Norwegian winter. Its performance exceeded expectations. Meanwhile, Sweden has unveiled a hydrogen snowplow that is, in fact, another large battery-electric truck, with a fuel cell and hydrogen tanks added for extra range. The engineering question is why that second energy system is worth having when batteries are already doing the work, and when a conventional generator running on renewable diesel could offer a simpler, potentially cheaper route to occasional extended operation.

The Swedish vehicle has to compete with more than diesel snowplows. My full TFIE Strategy Briefing examines Norway’s measured electric operation, China’s expanding snow-removal equipment market and the additional costs hydrogen must justify.

Sweden’s project brings together Scania, MaserFrakt and Peab. The vehicle carries a 356 kWh rechargeable battery and 56 kg of hydrogen. The fuel cell generates electricity to extend the truck’s operating time between charging sessions. That gives the vehicle two energy-storage systems, plus the equipment to convert hydrogen into electricity. It will still need electric charging, and it will also need hydrogen production, delivery, storage and refueling.

Norway’s experience makes the starting point uncomfortable for hydrogen advocates. The Norwegian Public Roads Administration’s 2025 trial demonstrated that a production-based heavy electric truck could do demanding winter-maintenance work. Its measured consumption averaged approximately 2.02 kWh/km, with around six and a half hours of operating endurance under evaluated mixed-duty conditions. The trial identified shortcomings in charging compatibility and payload, but these were engineering and operating problems to resolve, not evidence that battery-electric snowplows were incapable of doing the job.

China is moving toward broader deployment. Municipalities have used smaller electric snow-removal equipment for years, while manufacturers have developed full-sized specialized electric vehicles. Beijing’s Mentougou district awarded contracts for 24 multifunction snow-removal trucks in September 2026. The final chassis specifications have not all been confirmed as battery-electric, but the procurement demonstrates a market moving beyond isolated demonstrations.

China’s much larger battery-electric truck industry is also providing specialized equipment manufacturers with an expanding supply of powertrains, batteries and heavy-duty chassis. Electric snowplows benefit from components developed and manufactured for freight vehicles at much greater volumes.

The Swedish approach looks increasingly difficult to justify against that background. If six or seven hours of productive operation is adequate, a battery-electric truck can already do the work. If longer shifts are required, larger batteries, better charging arrangements, mobile charging equipment or operational changes deserve assessment first. Hydrogen cannot claim the extreme-duty market merely because charging requires planning.

There is another alternative that the hydrogen comparison tends to omit. A conventional generator running on hydrotreated vegetable oil, or HVO, could supply additional electricity when the battery needs support. Diesel generators, fuel tanks and liquid-fuel distribution systems are mature technologies. Major generator manufacturers already approve suitable equipment for HVO, which can use conventional diesel-type storage and handling systems. Integrating a generator into a particular electric truck still requires engineering, certification and emissions controls, but it avoids constructing a hydrogen supply chain for a small fleet of seasonal vehicles.

For some operators, the even easier solution is to retain existing diesel snow-removal equipment and use certified renewable diesel for the relatively few extreme shifts that electric vehicles cannot cover. Copenhagen Airport has already adopted that approach, progressively electrifying its equipment while using HVO in compatible heavy vehicles, including snow-removal machines.

HVO is not unlimited, and its climate benefits depend on feedstock origin and production. Burning it also produces exhaust emissions. These constraints are important, particularly in populated areas. But a relatively small quantity used for exceptional winter duty is a different proposition from trying to replace a large share of road transportation with biofuels.

The hydrogen proposal must beat all these alternatives. It needs to demonstrate that the additional hours gained from the fuel cell are worth the vehicle cost, maintenance, fuel premium and refueling infrastructure. It also needs to outperform the cost of providing those hours with conventional generating equipment or retaining a small reserve fleet.

Snow-removal authorities have an obligation to maintain roads during severe weather. They should purchase equipment that meets that obligation with the lowest defensible whole-system cost and emissions. Norway has shown that batteries can perform demanding winter work, and China’s industrial scale is making specialized electric vehicles more accessible. Sweden’s hydrogen truck is entering a market in which the simpler electric solution is already working.

The full TFIE Strategy Briefing analysis examines the operating results, procurement evidence, charging limitations, airport fuel-cell trials and the practical alternatives that make hydrogen’s business case so difficult.

#5724. Hardware-testing and engineering startup Nominal raises $240M at $3B valuation

Artificial intelligence-powered hardware-testing and engineering software startup Nominal Inc. today announced it has raised $240 million in new funding led by Lightspeed Venture Partners and Insight Partners.

The investment triples the company’s valuation to $3 billion, up from $1 billion cemented in March after it raised $80 million in a Series B-2 funding round. Additional major investors in the Series C round included Lux Capital, Sequoia, General Catalyst, Founders Fund, Avenir, Salesforce Ventures, M13 and Lockheed Martin Ventures.

Nominal assists engineers with hardware development by supporting testing and development. Engineers must piece together data from disconnected testing systems to understand how a machine performed under realistic conditions and understand what needs fixing.

The platform brings that information together, automates testing, and uses AI to help analyze the results. This shortens the cycle between testing and design, enabling faster improvements and iterations.

The challenge in the field isn’t collecting more data; there are plenty of ways to get that from simulation, sensors, video, and more. Hardware tests generate streams of sensor readings, logs, video and simulation results that all need to be analyzed together to create a whole picture of what happened. The company’s AI agent, Nominal Analyst, investigates that data and performs analysis based on the underlying evidence.

“Hardware engineering is getting its AI moment, with real operational value that goes far beyond making existing workflows faster,” said co-founder and Chief Executive Cameron McCord. “The companies building the world’s most advanced machines have decades of hard-won knowledge in their organizations.”

The company said it built its AI Intelligence Platform to bring together all the systems needed for testing and design assistance. It has multiple layers, including connections to engineering applications, the agent infrastructure, the data and finally the physical world through sensors.

Examples of what Nominal’s AI product works with alongside engineers include aircraft, rocket engines, autonomous vehicles, drones and energy systems. Engineering data and documentation associated with the hardware fed to the agents help during the development process to investigate performance, compare tests and check results against requirements.

The company said the challenge is putting engineers’ knowledge to work and connecting it to data so engineers can take on harder problems than wiring up tests. The objective is to let them sit down, smooth out challenges and address what looked impossible before.

“Engineers stay in command, with purpose-built AI helping them do their best work,” added McCord.

Nominal works with the tools engineers already bring, including application programming interfaces, Model Context Protocol and SQL for database queries. Developers can also directly access the platform to connect tools, build custom applications, and create their own workflows and agents.

The company said more than 80 commercial and government organizations use its platform, including five of the seven biggest defense contractors. Nominal’s customers include defense technology company Anduril Industries Inc., military shipbuilder Huntington Ingalls Industries Inc., known as HII, and high-speed aircraft developer Hermeus Corp.

#5723. NASA Pushes Further Ahead With The Non-Space Side Of Its Mission, Teases New Experimental Plane

NASA has unveiled, sort of, its newest experimental plane. And by that, the agency appears to mean a plane meant to conduct experiments, rather than the plane itself being the experiment. Called the X-70 Fractal, the aircraft's primary selling point is its modular design, both inside and out. This means that payloads can be swapped out easily, whether they are hanging off the wings or nestled inside the plane. Even the flight controls can be reconfigured in case the agency wants to test different ways for the pilots (and it is piloted) to maneuver. The X-70 is really a platform to allow for a wide array of experiments on a single airframe, rather than creating a bespoke airframe to conduct one mission, like the X-59 is doing now.

As for the plane itself, the X-70 Fractal is... well, more announcement than vehicle, at least for now. NASA says that it can carry 2,000 pounds of science equipment and take off with up to 10,000 pounds total. It will fly up to 45,000 feet in altitude, far above most airliners and well into the stratosphere. It will go up to 1,500 nautical miles, broadly on par with an F-35. It also looks like an F-35, I think, maybe? For images, all we've got is this misty photo that looks AI generated. NASA seems to want to copy the energy of the F-47 and F/A-XX reveals, which are also foggy renderings and not actual photographs. Show me you're making an airplane without showing me you're making an airplane, I guess.

NASA achieves such historic feats in space that it's easy to forget that it is also an "Aeronautics" administration. Part of its remit is to push forward the boundaries of aviation here on this planet, which NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman has renewed focus on. Isaacman himself is a pilot who owns his own MiG-29 Soviet fighter jet, so this is an area of personal interest for him. In fact, he's promising that more experimental aircraft are on their way; rumors abound that the agency may be returning the famous SR-71 Blackbird, the fastest plane ever made, to service.

By doing so, NASA does important R&D on airplane technology that is then released into the public record, to the benefit of all aviation companies and everyone who flies on their products. That's the whole point of the X-59, which is trying to reduce the impact of sonic booms enough to make commercial supersonic planes financially viable. In addition, NASA's latest budget points to aviation as an area of strategic competition, per Wired. To that end, it may do some research alongside the Pentagon as well. This is where something like the X-70 is useful: it could do scientific, commercial, or military research as needed, simply by swapping out equipment payloads via its modular design. Now all NASA needs to do is, you know, build it, possibly with a contractor. Details!

#5722. Another Drug Shows Potential for Functional Cures in Chronic Hepatitis B

— With highest dose of siRNA therapy, 19% achieved a functional cure 24 weeks after treatment ended

Reductions in hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) were observed with a novel small interfering RNA (siRNA) therapy in patients with chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection, according to a phase II study.

Among patients randomized to monotherapy with one of four doses of the siRNA HRS-5635, all 32 on the highest dose (400 mg) had HBsAg levels less than 100 IU/mL after 48 weeks of treatment, with 88% still at that level 24 weeks after treatment ended.

Among this high-dose group, 16% achieved a functional cure, with an HBsAg clearance level of less than 0.05 IU/mL after 48 weeks -- a percentage that rose to 19% by 24 weeks post-treatment, reported Xieer Liang, PhD, of Southern Medical University in Guangzhou, China, at the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases annual meeting in Denver.

"A dose-dependent antiviral response was observed with HRS-5635," Liang said. "All HRS-5635 regimens were generally safe and well-tolerated."

An estimated 240 million people worldwide have chronic HBV infection, including about 640,000 U.S. adults. Chronic HBV can cause liver damage, cirrhosis, liver cancer, and death. Five antivirals and two immune modulators are approved in the U.S. to treat chronic HBV, with treatment regimens lasting from 6 months to over 1 year.

In a previous phase II trial, siRNA therapy with an immunomodulator reduced HBsAg in patients with chronic HBV infection. Last month, the FDA approved another nucleic acid-based therapeutic, the antisense oligonucleotide drug bepirovirsen (Hibsago), for patients with chronic HBV taking antiviral therapy based on results from the B-Well 1 and B-Well 2 studies. In those trials, 19% to 20% of patients with HBsAg levels between 100 and 3,000 IU/mL had a functional cure with bepirovirsen at week 72.

The current trial included patients with chronic HBV on stable nucleos(t)ide analogue therapy who had HBsAg levels over 100 and less than 3,000 IU/mL and HBV DNA levels less than 20 IU/mL. Patients could be hepatitis B envelope antigen (HBeAg) positive or negative, but they couldn't have cirrhosis. All patients received tenofovir amibufenamide during 48 weeks of HRS-5635 treatment.

Mean age ranged from 41.5 to 44.6 years in the four treatment groups, 59.4% to 76.7% were men, and mean HBsAg ranged from 1,058.2 IU/mL to 1,200.4 IU/mL. Most patients were HBeAg negative (65.6% to 73.3%).

The investigators defined functional cure as sustained HBV DNA suppression and HBsAg clearance of less than 0.05 IU/mL, with or without seroconversion, sustained for 24 weeks after treatment.

All four HRS-5635 doses achieved the study's primary endpoint of HBsAg reduction from baseline to week 12, with mean reductions of -1.26 log10 IU/mL in the 50-mg group, -1.90 log10 IU/mL in the 100-mg group, -1.99 log10 IU/mL in the 200-mg group, and -2.12 log10 IU/mL in the 400-mg group.

Among patients in the 400-mg group, 45% converted from HBeAg positive to HBeAg negative after 48 weeks of treatment, a percentage that slid to 27% at 24 weeks after treatment.

In patients receiving the 400-mg dose who were HBeAg negative and had HBsAg below 1,000 IU/mL at baseline, 33% reached the functional cure rate of HBsAg less than 0.05 IU/mL.

Across the four groups, 46.9% to 60% had a treatment-related adverse event. There were only two such events that were grade 3 or higher, and no serious adverse events related to treatment and no deaths occurred. Upper respiratory tract infections were the most common adverse event, occurring in 25% to 33.3% of patients in the four groups.

Alanine transaminase elevations occurred in up to 6.7% of patients during and after treatment, Liang said, but levels were generally stable during treatment, and no elevations reached a grade 3 level.

The follow-up period of 24 weeks after treatment ended was relatively short, Liang cautioned, but a longer-duration extension study is ongoing, along with a phase III trial.

#5721. RFK Jr. Is Ushering in Peptides. As an Oncologist, Here Are My Concerns.

— Clinical evidence hasn't caught up with commercial enthusiasm

On July 13, 2025, at a Las Vegas hotel hosting the Revolution Against Aging and Death Festival, two women were taken away in ambulances. Both had received injections containing experimental peptides at a conference booth. Both became seriously ill and required ventilators. One mixture was believed to contain MOTS-c, P21, BPC-157, and TB4, substances promoted for tissue repair, metabolic health, and longevity.

Both women recovered. Nevada regulators subsequently imposed $35,000 in fines on four parties involved. But investigators could not establish what caused the reactions. They were unable to obtain the injected products for laboratory testing, and their exact contents remain unverified.

That is what bothers me most: two women experienced life-threatening reactions, and investigators could not determine precisely what they received.

Now, Washington is opening a regulatory path for some of these unproven peptides. On October 28, HHS announced an interim enforcement-discretion policy covering six peptides: BPC-157, MOTS-c, TB-500, KPV, Semax, and Epitalon. Under specified conditions, the government does not intend to take enforcement action against licensed pharmacies and physicians compounding these substances while the FDA considers formal rulemaking.

This is not an FDA approval, and it does not establish safety or effectiveness. While the HHS policy includes safeguards that represent progress, the policy also permits wider access before clinical evidence has caught up with commercial enthusiasm.

The question is not whether peptides have therapeutic potential. Many of them do. The question is whether that potential justifies their use before we know whether they work and are safe. The policy followed a July meeting of the FDA's Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee, which voted eight to six with one abstention, to recommend BPC-157 for the compounding list. It also endorsed five of the other six substances considered.

FDA reviewers had reached a different conclusion. Their briefing documents found insufficient evidence to support adding any of the seven substances. For BPC-157, evaluated for ulcerative colitis, they could not establish effectiveness. For several others, including TB-500, KPV, MOTS-c, and Epitalon, human safety studies were absent or extremely limited. Reviewers also identified problems with product characterization.

I have spent much of my career conducting oncology trials, including studies contributing to immunotherapies and targeted agents that are now used worldwide. I have seen promising mechanisms fail to translate into patient benefit and unexpected toxicities emerge after treatments entered routine practice. Clinical development is slow, expensive, and often disappointing. But it is how we distinguish a promising hypothesis from a useful medicine. We should make the review process more efficient, not bypass it.

I see a particular oncologic concern with the premature movement on peptides. Experimental studies suggest BPC-157 may stimulate angiogenesis, the formation of new blood vessels, through pathways involving VEGFR2 and endothelial nitric oxide synthase. Angiogenesis supports normal tissue repair. It is also a process many tumors exploit to sustain growth. This does not mean BPC-157 causes cancer or promotes tumor progression -- we lack human evidence to make that claim. But neither can we definitively exclude such effects, particularly with prolonged exposure or in patients with existing or previously treated malignancies.

In oncology, we routinely encounter treatments acting on pathways shared by normal and malignant tissues. Biological activity beneficial in one setting may have unintended consequences in another. The response should not be to assume harm, but to investigate it.

There is also an indication mismatch. The FDA evaluated BPC-157 for ulcerative colitis, while much commercial interest concerns tendon injuries, exercise recovery, and anti-aging. Evidence for one indication cannot establish safety or effectiveness for another, particularly when doses, routes, and duration differ.

The HHS policy includes safeguards worth acknowledging: appropriately sourced ingredients, documentation of identity and purity, single-ingredient preparations, labeling, serious adverse-event reporting, and patient-specific prescriptions. These address genuine problems in the existing peptide market. Patients already obtain experimental substances through poorly regulated online suppliers. Licensed compounding under defined conditions could reduce some risks.

But we must distinguish between three questions:

Manufacturing controls help answer the first one. Toxicology and clinical studies address the second. Well-designed trials establish the third. A certificate of analysis cannot demonstrate effectiveness. A prescription does not establish a favorable benefit-risk ratio. Adverse-event reporting cannot replace prospective safety studies.

Compounding serves an important clinical purpose, meeting individual needs when commercial formulations are unsuitable. But it should not replace drug development. When experimental peptides are marketed through wellness clinics, telehealth, and social media to thousands of patients for similar purposes, they begin to resemble commercial drugs, even when prescriptions are individualized.

The same principle applies to longevity medicine. Research into cellular senescence, mTOR signaling, metabolic regulation, and cellular reprogramming offers genuine opportunities. I welcome it. But results in mice do not establish human benefit, and widespread use without systematic study does not necessarily generate reliable knowledge. We should accelerate research, not replace it with uncontrolled experimentation.

The HHS policy remains interim, with public comments invited through November 13. That process should address dosing, clinical benefit, long-term safety, adverse-event surveillance, and opportunities to link expanded access to systematic evidence generation.

The choice is not between innovation and regulation. Good regulation enables innovation while protecting patients from uncertain benefits and risks. We have learned this repeatedly in cancer drug development: a compelling mechanism begins a research program. It does not prove a drug is effective.

Innovation deserves encouragement. And patients deserve evidence.

#5719. Cutaneous Sarcoidosis Could Soon Get an Effective Therapy

— Drug already approved for dermatomyositis passes phase II test

ORLANDO -- Patients with cutaneous sarcoidosis -- a condition with no very effective therapy -- saw dramatic improvement with the dual-acting TYK2/JAK1 inhibitor brepocitinib (Lisraya) in a small phase II trial.

Patients treated with either of two doses of brepocitinib achieved 22-point reductions in Cutaneous Sarcoidosis Activity and Morphology Instrument-Activity (CSAMI-A) scores after 16 weeks, well above the 5-point threshold for clinical relevance, compared with no decrease at all with placebo, reported Misha Rosenbach, MD, of the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia, and colleagues.

The drug also showed strong efficacy for secondary outcomes, the group found, and no serious adverse effects were recorded. The study was published in JAMA Dermatology and was also presented here at the American College of Rheumatology annual meeting.

Cutaneous sarcoidosis might be the biggest treatment challenge in all of dermatology. Corticosteroids have long been the mainstay of therapy, but are only sporadically effective and, among patients who do respond, relapses are common. Second-line treatments such as hydroxychloroquine, methotrexate, or tetracyclines don't do much better. Tumor necrosis factor (TNF) inhibitors were recommended as third-line therapy in a 2021 treatment guideline, but on very poor evidence. A French case series published in 2017 suggested TNF inhibitors could be used effectively, but the authors noted that adverse effects and discontinuations were common, and one-third of patients relapsed while on therapy.

With this dismal treatment landscape in mind, clinicians have turned to Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors as a possible alternative. Drugs such as tofacitinib (Xeljanz) and upadacitinib (Rinvoq) have been tried with some success, but only in single case reports and small series. Good results were also reported last year with the currently approved TYK2 inhibitor deucravacitinib (Sotyktu) in one patient.

All that bodes well for brepocitinib, which the FDA approved in August for dermatomyositis, and the phase II data in sarcoidosis appear to bear out the promise. Rosenbach and colleagues enrolled 31 patients, randomizing them in a 3:2:2 ratio to 45 or 15 mg/day of brepocitinib or placebo; they could stay on their conventional non-targeted therapies, but oral steroids were withdrawn over the first 8 weeks and topical steroids were stopped at randomization.

Patients were generally in their 40s and 50s. Mean disease duration varied in the three arms: about 10 years for the placebo and high-dose brepocitinib groups, and 4 years in the low-dose group. CSAMI-A scores averaged about 34 at baseline. Roughly 40% of participants had lupus pernio, the lumpy discolored facial and cranial lesions that may be the worst symptom of cutaneous sarcoidosis. Pulmonary sarcoidosis was also common in the sample.

Change from baseline in CSAMI-A score was the primary outcome measure. While no difference between the two brepocitinib doses was seen for this endpoint, "high-bar" outcomes showed some gaps. All patients in the high-dose group saw at least 10-point reductions in CSAMI-A scores, compared with 73% on the low dose (and 14% in the placebo group). Similarly, "functional remission," defined as a score below 5, was achieved by 62% with 45 mg versus 46% on 15 mg, and none receiving placebo.

Perhaps most encouragingly, all five patients in the 45-mg group with lupus pernio achieved 10-point reductions in CSAMI-A scores. Patients on the active drug also had substantial improvement in skin-related quality of life, whereas the placebo group actually had deterioration. (The near-total lack of improvement with placebo for any efficacy outcome testifies to just how difficult cutaneous sarcoidosis is to treat.)

With regard to safety, one patient in each arm quit therapy because of adverse events. But none were rated as serious. One patient on 45 mg showed a creatinine kinase elevation, and one developed anemia. Otherwise, no "special interest" events were seen; these included cardiovascular events, viral reactivation, transaminase elevations, venous thromboembolism, and malignancies.

Following his conference presentation, Rosenbach was asked where brepocitinib might fit in the treatment algorithm for cutaneous sarcoidosis. He cautioned that it was still early to speculate on that, since a larger phase III trial is only just getting underway. But if those data are like those he reported, "I imagine many patients would get it as first line," he said.

He was also asked about effects on pulmonary and joint manifestations, which are common in cutaneous sarcoidosis. He said the studies thus far have really focused on skin, and he couldn't say much about other symptoms. He added, though, that these would almost certainly be examined in the phase III trial.

Brepocitinib's developer, Priovant Therapeutics, expects primary results from the phase III study at the end of 2028. Rosenbach said the 45-mg dose will be the one tested for potential approval. Additional trials are underway in uveitis and lichen planopilaris; there's no indication, however, that Priovant plans to challenge deucravacitinib, which is approved for plaque psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis.
