#5718. On theCUBE Pod: Blue wave sends AI stock plunging

The very blue results of last week’s midterms have sent technology investors into a tailspin.

With many successful candidates running on platforms opposing data centers and calling for greater restrictions on artificial intelligence, investors anticipate a slowdown in AI spending. Tech stocks fell, with a collective loss of $2.5 trillion in market cap, and the Nasdaq dropped more than 5.5%.

“Yesterday was a bloodbath,” said John Furrier (pictured), executive analyst for theCUBE Research. “It was brutal here and the tech stocks got pounded. 41 states had data centers on the ballot. They all lost or won, depending how you look at it. Now it’s so mainstream, it’s a political football. So you’re starting to see the reality of AI. It’s hitting everybody. Everyone is impacted.”

On the latest episode of theCUBE Pod, Furrier and Dave Vellante (pictured, right), chief analyst for theCUBE Research, discussed the fallout from the midterms and whether or not AI companies will really suffer in the long term. They also explored who will own the “system of intelligence” that will govern enterprise AI.

After the “bloodbath” last week, the question remains: Can enterprise AI pay for the boom? Despite the shockwaves from the midterms, theCUBE’s researchers are predicting a longer path toward monetization. A recent analysis identified 2029 as the highest-risk year for the AI bubble.

“There’s a clock in terms of the data center monetization and financing and how long it takes to build data centers,” Vellante said. “We know anybody who can sell GPUs is making money but the enterprises aren’t yet self-funding. I had said that by 2026, this year, you’re going to start to see clear evidence of monetization in the enterprise. I think you see it, but you’re seeing it within tech companies.”

Tech companies are applying AI more effectively, according to Vellante, which should not come as a surprise. He thinks the tech titans are in a solid position while neoclouds are taking on a greater share of risk by pioneering a new software model, although not all of them will make it in the long term.

A GPU-based AI economy will shift in the next several years, Furrier believes, which could lead to surprising winners and losers.

“Supermicro [Inc.], good numbers, [Advanced Micro Devices Inc., Arista Networks, Marvell Technology Inc.],” he noted. “My take is this: the infrastructure is evolving beyond GPU-centric computing. Networking, optics, memory, storage, power efficiency. System-level architecture is becoming the strategic advantage, and those bottlenecks are being solved by the companies I just mentioned. You saw the news that Marvell closed a $115 billion acquisition of Lumentum.”

The stock market plunge shows that not everyone is going to make it through the AI era’s eventual slowdown. Public opinion on data centers is mixed, to say the least, so companies will need to establish a foothold in the developing system of AI intelligence to remain competitive.

“Neoclouds like CoreWeave are going to make it through,” Vellante said. “They’re the first movers and they’ve got some quality advantages but they’re going to go through some pain. Hyperscalers are like an ATM. They could dial it down at any point in time … but right now it’s all about growth, it’s about footprint, it’s about market share.”

Who owns the “system of intelligence”? This layer, which will bridge the gap between intelligent agents and the data systems they depend on, appears to still be in play. Palantir Technologies Inc. has the ontology that could give it the edge, while Snowflake Inc. and Databricks Inc. are still developing the operational systems — though Vellante sees the latter as having one of the best strategies.

“You need determinism to own that system of intelligence,” Vellante said. “So I think it’s wide open. Right now, I think Ali Ghodsi [chief executive officer of Databricks] has the best vision. He’s going after the client surface, he’s going after the system of intelligence, he’s going after the governance catalog, he’s going after the agent action layer, and he’s partnering … with all the frontier model vendors. Whether or not they can pull it off, we’ll see.”

Frontier models are the “wild card,” as Vellante puts it, but at the moment, all the tech companies are trying to get a slice of the pie. Despite the recent market shakeups, Furrier sees AI-native enterprises as the ultimate result of this current period of growth.

“The AI-native enterprise or businesses is going to be the model,” Furrier said. “Everybody wins in that one. Compute providers, hyperscalers, the data platforms that are on the right side, and the application companies, which are basically going to be agentic. That’s going to be the winners on the profit concentration. The control point … it’s not going to be the models, it’s going to be data and context, and the agents will be the proof point.”

Tom Lee, investor and entrepreneur Dan Ives, technology analyst Frank Slootman, former chairman of the board of directors at Snowflake Inc. Ali Ghodsi, co-founder and chief executive officer of Databricks John Roese, global CTO and chief AI officer of Dell Technologies Lisa Su, chair and CEO of AMD Michael Dell, chairman and CEO of Dell Technologies George Gilbert, principal analyst at theCUBE Research Geoffrey Moore, principal at Geoffrey Moore Consulting Rob Hof, editor-in-chief at SiliconANGLE Media Stu Miniman, senior director of market insights, hybrid platforms, at Red Hat

#5717. Enfortumab Vedotin-Based Treatment Solidified for Muscle-Invasive Bladder Cancer

— Experts discuss survival gains and whether all patients need adjuvant therapy

In this exclusive roundtable video from MedPage Today, three expert leaders in the field of bladder cancer discuss the latest emerging data presented at the European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO) congress.

Moderator Matthew Galsky, MD, of the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in New York City, is joined by David Aggen, MD, PhD, of Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York City, and Stephanie Berg, DO, of the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute in Boston.

In this first of four episodes, they examine findings from the VOLGA trial, including the survival benefits of enfortumab vedotin (EV; Padcev) plus durvalumab (Imfinzi) and whether all patients need additional treatment following cystectomy.

Following is a transcript of their remarks:

Galsky: Hi everyone. Welcome to MedPage Today ESMO Roundtable on [genitourinary] cancers. And I'm Matt Galsky. I'm a medical oncologist focusing on bladder cancer at the Tisch Cancer Institute at Mount Sinai in New York. And I'm joined today by Dr. David Aggen from Memorial Sloan Kettering and Dr. Stephanie Berg from the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute. So welcome both of you. Thanks for joining.

Galsky: Absolutely. We had a pretty consequential set of data from ESMO this year on localized bladder cancer, both muscle-invasive disease and non-muscle-invasive disease. So over the next bit of time, I thought we would talk about some of the more important data, some of the potential practice-changing or practice-informing data, and would love to get your opinion on a set of studies that I think probably are the most important to talk about. And by the end of the discussions, I'm hoping that each of us can identify maybe immediate practice implication related to the data or an unanswered research question that you think should be tackled next.

So I thought we'd start with VOLGA, and I was going to present just a brief overview of the VOLGA study for the audience, and then would love to get your input on VOLGA. So just as a bit of context, we all know that from the KEYNOTE-905 and KEYNOTE-B15 studies in cisplatin-ineligible and cisplatin-eligible patients, respectively, that the regimen of perioperative enfortumab vedotin plus pembrolizumab [Keytruda] with cystectomy is a standard treatment approach for patients with muscle-invasive bladder cancer.

VOLGA tested a variation on this theme. So VOLGA enrolled patients who were cisplatin-ineligible or -declining and patients were randomized to receive either cystectomy alone, as was considered a standard of care at the time, or neoadjuvant treatment with enfortumab vedotin plus durvalumab for three cycles and then adjuvant durvalumab.

So a couple of differentiators from KEYNOTE-905: one, the use of durvalumab rather than pembrolizumab. The second is that in the adjuvant phase of treatment, there was no enfortumab vedotin given, which there was in KEYNOTE-905. In this study, it was only adjuvant immune checkpoint blockade. There was a third arm of the study and that included tremelimumab [Imjudo], a few doses of tremelimumab in the neoadjuvant and then one dose in the adjuvant setting, I believe.

The triplet regimen with tremelimumab demonstrated an improvement in disease-free survival, or event-free survival [EFS] rather, but not an improvement in overall survival [OS] -- yet. But the regimen of enfortumab vedotin plus durvalumab showed an improvement in event-free survival and an improvement in overall survival. The hazard ratios look pretty good, 0.51 for OS, 0.58. I'm sorry, 0.51 for EFS and 0.58 for overall survival. And I didn't really comment on the path CR [pathologic complete response] rates in the study, but would love to get your thoughts on that as well.

So Dr. Aggen, what do you think of this study? What does it add to the treatment of patients with muscle-invasive bladder cancer?

Aggen: I think that VOLGA really solidifies that enfortumab vedotin with a checkpoint is the standard for patients with muscle-invasive disease. The two phase III trials now in cisplatin-ineligible patients showing a huge benefit in terms of event-free and overall survival to giving neoadjuvant therapy.

I do think a couple key takeaways are that it's unclear the adjuvant contribution of enfortumab vedotin for some patients, and VOLGA really brings that into question, that some patients may not need enfortumab vedotin for an extended course after surgery. It's really on us to figure out who those patients are. There seems to be comparable EFS with a more limited duration of EV therapy.

The second thing though that's sort of of interest is the pathologic complete response rate in VOLGA, which was about 45% by investigator assessment and then closer to 40% actually when it was centrally reviewed. That is slightly lower than what we saw with all the caveats of cross-trial comparisons in EV-303/KEYNOTE-905 and EV304/KEYNOTE-B15.

And so I do think that's something that we're going to be talking about. A key theme of the meeting though in some of the other trials we may discuss later on is that path CR rate doesn't necessarily equate with long-term outcome. There were path CR rates with pembrolizumab in combination with cisplatin on the order of about 44% reported, and that did not equate to the same EFS and OS benefit.

So for me, the key takeaway is that for a patient with muscle-invasive disease, we should be having a conversation about ADC-IO [antibody-drug conjugate and immuno-oncology] therapy. I think that the onus is on us to figure out how much and who needs additional adjuvant treatment based on which regimen you select.

Galsky: Thank you. Dr. Berg, so Dr. Aggen mentioned that not everyone might need adjuvant EV, maybe not everyone needs adjuvant immune checkpoint blockade. Are there criteria that you use in clinic right now to determine what to do after surgery?

Berg: I think right now I'm still using the trial criteria and offering adjuvant, at least immunotherapy, and EV for those I think that can tolerate it. We all know radical cystectomy is quite tough and if you can try to get it in the window of time, but I completely agree with high-risk disease, it's important. But then if they have path CR or low risk, still T1 with a treatment effect, you really question is adjuvant anything needed, especially adjuvant EV.

And when you think about toxicities, like Dr. Aggen mentioned, especially with peripheral neuropathy, thankfully they were getting less EV in VOLGA, just the three cycles, but that can be really life-changing for patients and it's something that we really have to think about. What are we going to be doing for them if we eliminated micrometastasis and increasing that risk for permanent toxicity? So it's something I think the question isn't completely answered, but I think this data really helped at least bridge a little bit of the gap about having a broader discussion about adjuvant EV, and we're going to hopefully see some trials in this space.

And I just wanted to add that this also made me realize, and to tell our patients, that you can still get neoadjuvant treatment and go to surgery. I think it just confirmed that it's not really leading to more complications and it's really established how we're doing, as Dr. Aggen said, EV and ICI [immune checkpoint inhibitor], because I think we're not saying ICI specific now, and I'm sure once NCCN [National Comprehensive Cancer Network] gets a hold of it, we'll have a different wording for that language.

Galsky: Dr. Aggen, what do you make of the CTLA-4 blockade data? Sort of a checkered history in urothelial cancer so far.

Aggen: Unfortunately, it's been difficult to see a clear long-term benefit with CTLA-4 and bladder cancer like we've seen historically in kidney cancer. And it seems that the additional toxicity doesn't necessarily equate to an improvement in terms of pathologic complete response rates and not yet in terms of overall survival. Probably there's a subgroup of patients with immune-infiltrated tumors maybe that could benefit from CTLA-4, but I just don't think we have a clear sense of who those patients are at the moment.

Galsky: Thank you. So maybe one quick take home from both of you regarding VOLGA. How does this impact your practice Monday morning?

Berg: I can go first. I would say it fits in a sense that I'm going to say without cisplatin eligibility, I'm going to offer EV and ICI for patients prior to radical cystectomy if that's what they're choosing for their perioperative care. And that's what I'm going to go with.

Aggen: I think that if 10 years ago, Matt, we told Dean Bajorin that we'd have hazard ratios of 0.51 in muscle-invasive disease, he would've had a hard time believing us. I think that VOLGA reaffirms that ADC-IO therapy is the backbone of neoadjuvant therapy. And there's going to be, I think, a lot of shared decision making when it comes to adjuvant therapy. Certainly for patients with residual disease at cystectomy, those are patients who in my mind absolutely should continue ADC-IO therapy postoperatively.

Galsky: And I think you make a great point. We have two contemporary studies now with comparisons of systemic therapy with cystectomy versus cystectomy alone. It's pretty unusual to have that in solid tumors in this age where systemic therapy is integrated into clinically-localized disease across the board. So there's really no surgery-alone trials anymore.

So two contemporary studies both showing marked improvement in outcomes with perioperative systemic therapy. I think that really sort of seals the question about whether or not perioperative systemic therapy is needed in muscle-invasive bladder cancer. So thank you for those comments.

#5716. Scientists discover that cranberry juice may help fight tooth decay

Cranberry juice may offer an unexpected benefit for your teeth. New research suggests that pure, unsweetened cranberry juice can slow the growth of dental plaque and reduce the production of acids that contribute to tooth decay.

Cranberries are a familiar part of holiday celebrations. They appear in sauces, salads, and cocktails, and even serve as colorful seasonal decorations. But beyond their tart flavor and festive appeal, these small red berries contain natural compounds that may support oral health.

Christine Wu, a researcher at the University of Illinois Chicago College of Dentistry, has been investigating whether cranberry juice could help protect teeth from harmful bacteria. Her findings suggest that the popular beverage may have benefits that go beyond its traditional association with urinary tract health.

How Cranberry Juice Affects Harmful Bacteria

Cranberry juice has long been used to help prevent urinary tract infections. One reason is that cranberries contain compounds called proanthocyanidins, which have anti-inflammatory properties and can interfere with the ability of certain bacteria, including E. coli, to attach to cells.

Wu wanted to determine whether these same compounds might also affect bacteria found in dental plaque. These microorganisms feed on sugars from food and drinks, producing acids that gradually weaken tooth enamel and contribute to cavities.

Rather than testing isolated cranberry compounds, Wu chose to investigate pure cranberry juice, a product people can readily purchase and consume.

"Just like sugar damage is linked to diet, I'm interested in how the food and beverages we consume can help combat the harmful bacteria and benefit our oral health," Wu said.

To investigate the potential effects, researchers conducted a small human study involving 22 participants, including 14 children and eight adults.

Participants were randomly assigned to one of three beverages: pure, unsweetened 100% cranberry juice, a cranberry juice cocktail containing 27% juice and added sugar, or plain water.

"It was important to us to conduct these tests with human participants and use products available on the market. Most cranberry juice studies have been conducted using laboratory-prepared cranberry juice extract. Moreover, limited studies have been performed in children," said Wu, who is a professor of pediatric dentistry.

On the morning of the experiment, participants arrived with dental plaque that had accumulated overnight. Researchers first collected plaque samples using cotton swabs on one side of each participant's mouth.

After rinsing with water, participants consumed three small amounts of their assigned beverage. They swished each drink around their mouths several times before swallowing.

Thirty minutes later, researchers collected another set of plaque samples, this time from teeth that had not been swabbed earlier. Comparing the samples allowed the team to examine how each beverage affected plaque activity over the short testing period.

A Surprising Effect on Plaque and Tooth Decay

The results revealed a promising effect of pure cranberry juice. Dental plaque exposed to the unsweetened beverage showed slower regrowth than unexposed plaque samples.

Researchers also found that swishing with pure cranberry juice reduced acid production in dental plaque from both children and adults. This is particularly important because acids produced by oral bacteria can gradually erode tooth enamel, increasing the risk of cavities.

The findings suggest that cranberry juice may interfere with two important processes involved in tooth decay: the buildup of bacterial plaque and the production of damaging acids.

Wu believes these results could eventually support the development of cranberry juice as a "functional beverage" that offers benefits for oral health. The findings are especially interesting because other commonly consumed fruit juices, including orange and apple juice, have not shown the same promise in this research context.

"Most people think of cranberry juice as very sour, very acidic and sugary, and therefore may not contribute positively to oral health. This study found the opposite: that cranberry juice affected dental plaque regrowth and acid production, which may counteract some of the damage done by sugar," she said.

Could Cranberry Juice Become Part of Oral Care?

Although the findings are encouraging, the researchers emphasize that further investigation is necessary. With only 22 participants and a testing period lasting just 30 minutes after consumption, the study cannot establish whether drinking cranberry juice regularly prevents cavities or produces lasting improvements in dental health.

Larger studies conducted over longer periods will be needed to determine whether the observed changes in dental plaque translate into meaningful protection against tooth decay.

Still, Wu sees potential in occasionally using pure cranberry juice as a mouth rinse. One challenge is its intensely tart flavor, which some people may find unpleasant without added sweetness.

"But maybe by adding an appropriate sugar substitute," she said, "to make it a bit more palatable."

The research was published in the journal Scientific Reports.

Materials provided by University of Illinois Chicago. Original written by Jenna Kurtzweil. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5715. Omada Health hikes 2026 outlook after ‘strongest quarter ever’ in Q3

Omada Health hikes 2026 outlook after ‘strongest quarter ever’ in Q3" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Omada Health saw its "strongest quarter ever" in the third quarter of 2026, CEO and co-founder Sean Duffy told investors and analysts during a Thursday evening earnings call.

"We delivered our highest quarterly revenue, gross margin progression, and our most profitable quarter to date," Duffy said.

The virtual chronic care provider, which went public last June, brought in $91 million in revenue—up 34% year-over-year—and reported gross margin of 76% on a GAAP basis and 78% on a non-GAAP basis, according to Duffy. Omada reported net income of $7 million in the third quarter, compared with a net loss of $3 million in Q3 2025.

The company also reported adjusted EBITDA of $12 million, compared to $2 million the year prior.

It beat Wall Street analysts’ estimates for revenue, though slightly trailed behind projections for total membership.

Total members reached 1.1 million, up 36% year-over-year, with trailing 12-month revenue per total member increasing 5% year-over-year to $294, according to financial results published Thursday. Average member tenure also grew 10% compared to the year prior, to approximately two years and four months. Member retention has improved to 58%, up from 43% in Q4 of 2024, executives said.

Omada Health President Wei-Li Shao said Q3 membership growth reflects "continued demand" for its cardiometabolic platform, adding that the company's diabetes and hypertension programs continued to lead growth.

The company's diabetes and hypertension programs, longer member retention and lower care delivery costs are increasingly driving both growth and profitability, executives said.

"Members stayed with us longer, and our ability to provide personalized care at scale reached a new level of efficiency," Shao said.

The company supports diabetes, hypertension, obesity and musculoskeletal conditions—launching a GLP-1 care companion solution last November.

Shao noted that Omada deepened its partnership with the Health Care Services Corporation (HCSC) last quarter to extend its prevention and hypertension programs into three additional states, which is expected to "potentially reach an additional estimated 1.5 million covered lives at launch in 2027."

"On the PBM side, we have commercial relationships with the three largest PBMs in the country, which together processed an estimated 80% of prescription claims in 2025," Shao said. "Our prescribing program is in the market now at Optum. These relationships give us the broadest distribution in Omada’s history for our programs."

Shao, who will take over as CEO Jan. 1, also noted that artificial intelligence solutions enable care teams to have more capacity to "apply their clinical expertise" while tailoring care to each member’s needs.

"This quarter shows what we have built at Omada," Shao said. "Our commercial relationships give us broad reach, and our cardiometabolic programs have driven growth. Our program mix has supported longer member tenure, and our cost to serve has decreased."

Chief Financial Officer Steve Cook told investors the company expects new enrollments to "moderate sequentially" in the fourth quarter, which he said is "consistent with historic seasonality."

Shao also noted that a number of employers have been spending more time making GLP-1 coverage and obesity care decisions, "given the size of the commitment, the range of solutions and the importance of getting these decisions right," which has extended the selling season deeper into the fourth quarter.

Omada Health's stock dropped 19% Friday following the Q3 earnings call on Thursday as investors pulled back due to concerns about the longer selling season and expected Q4 member decline clouding the company's 2027 outlook.

The company is raising its full 2026 revenue and adjusted EBITDA outlook. Cook said revenue is expected to range from $344 million to $346 million, up from its previous range of $334 million to $340 million. Adjusted EBITDA is expected to be in the range of $32 million to $34 million, up from $21 million to $27 million.

"Our outlook anticipates Q4 revenue below our Q3 level, reflecting the lower new enrollment and engagement activity we have historically seen during the holidays," Cook said. "We expect revenue to come primarily from continued engagement among existing members."

A Dutch trial found that equipping emergency medical services (EMS) with extracorporeal CPR technology, namely venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO), increased survival of people with refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. (New England Journal of Medicine)

The Society for Cardiovascular Angiography and Interventions SHOCK classification was updated to emphasize perfusion, serial reassessment, and clinical trajectory in describing cardiogenic shock severity. (JSCAI)

IV cangrelor (Kengreal) failed to meet noninferiority to crushed oral ticagrelor (Brilinta) for short-term clinical outcomes in a randomized trial of acute myocardial infarction complicated by cardiogenic shock. (The Lancet)

Compared with ezetimibe (Zetia), evolocumab (Repatha) was associated with a 20% lower rate of myocardial infarctions over 4 years, according to a target trial emulation study. (American Journal of Preventive Cardiology)

Early-stage data are promising for a strategy of extended aldosterone synthase inhibition, using a once-daily pill for a limited time, for remission from primary aldosteronism and its associated high blood pressure, said researchers at Queen Mary University of London.

Mineralys Therapeutics released 48-week results from the Transform-HTN open-label extension trial supporting lorundrostat for treatment of uncontrolled or resistant hypertension.

For people undergoing pulmonary vein isolation for persistent atrial fibrillation, adjunctive low-voltage area ablation did not reduce arrhythmia recurrence in the COAST-AF trial. (JAMA)

A single infusion of investigational factor XI inhibitors amrecibart or cenvacibart safely reduced the incidence of venous thromboembolism following peripherally inserted central catheter insertion, the ROXI-CATH phase II trial suggested. (Lancet Haematology)

More than a year after getting a heart transplant, patients initiating dapagliflozin (Farxiga) went on to have better estimated glomerular filtration rate trajectories. (Circulation)

In a real-world study of the cardiovascular safety of Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitors used for B-cell malignant neoplasms, there was 5.9% incidence of pericardial effusion or cardiac tamponade within about 2 years of treatment initiation. (JAMA Network Open)

#5713. Equiti acquires Lexi AI to combine AI, human medical interpretation

Equiti acquires Lexi AI to combine AI, human medical interpretation" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Equiti is acquiring Lexi AI to build a hybrid language-access model that combines AI language support with human medical interpreters.

Equiti, which sells medical interpretation services to hospitals and health systems through its Martti business, provides 24/7 access to qualified medical interpreters across more than 250 languages and dialects. Lexi provides multilingual, AI-powered medical interpretation. The acquisition deal merges Lexi's immediate AI language support, covering over 35 languages and dialects, with Martti and its network of qualified medical interpreters to help healthcare organizations expand language access.

The acquisition was announced October 28. Financial details of the deal were not disclosed.

With this acquisition, Equiti is building on Martti’s work pioneering video remote interpretation in healthcare more than two decades ago, according to executives. The use of AI can expand where and when language services can be offered, particularly for everyday interactions that may not currently receive interpretation support, Equiti executives said.

Martti was built alongside healthcare organizations to make qualified interpreters available by video. Lexi, in turn, has been developed with healthcare customers to extend immediate language support into more workflows. The acquisition brings those capabilities together, with human-in-the-loop design, patient safety and patient experience at its center, Equiti executives said.

The company saw an opportunity to combine its services with Lexi's AI expertise rather than build a healthcare AI interpretation product internally, Maureen Huber, Equiti CEO, told Fierce Healthcare.

"Lexi brings specialized expertise in AI, engineering and healthcare product design, along with experience putting that technology into the hands of care teams. That combination takes time to build," Huber said. "For more than 20 years, our work through Martti has been about making qualified human interpretation accessible within healthcare. We understand the service, the clinical environment and what it takes to support healthcare organizations every day. Developing AI and machine learning technology calls for additional, specialized expertise. We wanted people who had already been doing that work with healthcare in mind."

She added, "We spent time evaluating the category and learning from customers. Lexi brought together the people, product and approach we were seeking. Combining their expertise with ours gives us a stronger foundation to expand language access responsibly."

Combining AI and human interpretation makes language support more accessible across the patient journey, helping organizations improve care delivery while making better use of their resources, according to Equiti executives.

Healthcare organizations are increasingly interested in AI interpretation capabilities and are looking for guidance, Huber noted.

"Customers were asking: 'Where could AI help? How do we evaluate it? What is appropriate for our patients?' Healthcare leaders see the same advances in consumer AI that everyone else sees. They also must think about what happens when those tools enter a care environment, sometimes before an organization has decided how they should be used. They want a partner who understands both the possibilities and the responsibilities," she said.

She added, "I would describe that as inquiry and evaluation. There is real curiosity about extending language support to more of the patient experience, particularly before and after a visit. Our job is to help customers identify those opportunities while keeping qualified human interpretation central to care delivery."

Equiti calls this approach Modality Matters, a connected model that allows healthcare organizations to match each encounter with the appropriate modality — immediate, healthcare-purpose-built AI support for approved use cases and qualified medical interpretation where clinical complexity, regulatory requirements, organizational policy or patient preference calls for a human interpreter. With this approach, organizations have the flexibility to shift between modalities as clinical context and communication needs change in real time.

The combined portfolio of Equiti and Lexi's capabilities will extend language access into everyday interactions that often go unsupported, Huber noted.

Equiti is focusing Lexi's AI-powered medical interpretation on routine patient engagement, including before and after care, such as appointment communications, scheduling and nonclinical follow-up logistics.

"We see a significant opportunity for Lexi in that communication before and after care: helping patients exchange messages, arrange appointments and stay connected in their preferred language. Language access must extend beyond the clinical encounter. Think about what happens after a patient leaves the clinic. They receive a message about a follow-up appointment, but they need to ask whether it is at the same location, how to reschedule, or whom to contact. Those may be simple questions for the organization, but the answers determine whether the patient can take the next step," she said.

Qualified human interpreters remain the foundation for care delivery, Huber noted. "In conversations such as those about a diagnosis, informed consent, treatment or palliative care, the ability to clarify meaning, recognize cultural context and respond with empathy is essential. A medically qualified interpreter helps people understand one another through conversations that can be complex and deeply personal," she said.

Equiti said it can work with customers to define appropriate uses within their policies and applicable requirements, preserving patient choice and access to a qualified human interpreter.

Language access is also a strategic performance driver for healthcare organizations, as effective communication influences patient understanding and experience, clinical outcomes, workforce efficiency and financial performance.

Equiti's customers include Wellstar Health System, Corewell Health, NYU Langone and Lee Health. Lexi works with a growing pipeline of federally qualified health centers and community providers including Lowell Community Health Center, which serves one of the most multilingual communities in Massachusetts.

As general-purpose AI gets better at translation, a healthcare-specific interpretation platform has distinct advantages, Huber asserted.

"Healthcare communication involves clinical meaning, cultural context, jargon and acronyms during situations where people may be frightened, vulnerable or unsure how to ask a question. Our job is to remove those communication barriers, and that requires understanding the care environment, fitting into clinical workflows and knowing when a qualified human interpreter needs to be involved," she said. "That is where Equiti’s experience matters. We bring the relationships, service infrastructure and human expertise developed through more than two decades of healthcare interpretation, alongside Lexi’s technology and team."

Huber said she envisions broader uses of Lexi's AI language support in healthcare workflows. "A patient’s need to communicate continues after the conversation with a clinician ends. Lexi already supports text-based messaging, including translation of text provided by a care team, and can even leave voicemail messages for patients. That creates opportunities to help patients access information and communicate between visits. Helping someone navigate follow-up care is a natural direction for that work, like understanding the next step, connecting with the right office or arranging an appointment. The value is in making it easier for patients to act on the care plan they have been given and ask for help along the way," she said.

"We built Lexi to fit the way healthcare teams actually work, bringing immediate language support into the devices and workflows they already use,” Siddharth UR, co-founder and chief product officer of Lexi, said in a statement. “As part of Equiti, we can extend that experience across the patient journey and connect it to a broader language access model built around the needs of each encounter.”

Lexi will operate alongside Martti under Equiti, with the teams working together on implementation and integration across healthcare workflows. Equiti will work with each customer to determine how the solutions fit within its language access program, clinical environment, and organizational policies.

#5712. Cisco research: Trust, not technology, is now the speed limit on enterprise AI

GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala

For several years, the conversation about enterprise artificial intelligence has focused on capability: which model is smartest and which GPU is fastest. That made sense when technology was the constraint.

It isn’t anymore. AI can now do far more than most organizations will allow, and the gap is trust.

That’s the core finding of “Permission to Scale: The Critical Role of Trust in Successful AI Adoption,” new research released today at Cisco Systems Inc.’s Cisco Live APJC in Melbourne. Authored by independent researcher Brad Howarth, the study draws on data from 25 Australian organizations.

At Cisco Live APJC, Cisco hosted a press panel to discuss the report. The panel, moderated by Howarth, featured a number of corporate leaders from companies that participated in the report, including Carl Solder, chief technology officer of Cisco ANZ (far left); Anna Tosky, chief people officer at Elmo Software (second from left); Chris Locke, CTO at Flight Center Travel Group (third from left); Naz Wilson, group culture and enablement manager at Funlab (third from right); and Lucio Ribeiro, chief AI officer at TBWA Australia (second from right).

Though a sample size of 25 is small, the results align with conversations I’ve had with corporate leadership. I appreciated the panel’s mix of technologies, human resources and cultural leadership. I also valued the mix of roles, as the biggest barrier to scaling AI isn’t technical but people-related.

Australia makes an interesting test case. According to University of Melbourne and KPMG research cited in the report, half of Australians use AI regularly, but only 36% trust it, and just 30% believe its benefits outweigh its risks. That’s the lowest among 47 countries surveyed. If you can build trust in AI in Australia, that work will scale globally. In the press release, Stefan Leitl, vice president and general manager of Cisco Australia and New Zealand, discussed the benefits of winning over this region: “It’s a playbook that travels well beyond Australia.”

Solder noted that among the six pillars in Cisco’s AI Readiness Index, chief information officers and CTOs gravitate toward what they know, namely infrastructure and data, and leave culture for others. He described a customer that invested in infrastructure, governance, data and information technology skills but “didn’t focus on the culture. And they found that there was a big pushback from their employees and customers on using the toolsets they’ve invested in.”

This is something I’ve seen repeatedly: Companies spend millions on AI platforms only to see utilization remain tepid. Howarth discussed an adoption “flywheel” in which successful use creates evidence, evidence builds trust and trust enables broader use. Companies sit around waiting for trust before deploying, and the evidence of trust must be something measurable.

Trust in AI needs to be established with realistic parameters. Many people reject AI after a single mistake, even though in most cases the error rate is much lower than that of people. This mirrors what the automotive industry went through when a Tesla accident would trigger a media storm. The reality is that Tesla’s Autopilot system experiences one crash for about every 7 million miles, compared with human drivers, who average about one crash every 1 million miles.

Perfection isn’t a realistic goal, but being faster and more accurate than others is. Users should understand this going into any kind of trial or proof of concept, as the expectation of perfection can erode trust.

Chris Locke offered a great example of an executive leading by example. The company’s 77-year-old founder, Graham “Skroo” Turner, uses AI every day. “He’s a big Anthropic Claude user,” Locke said. “This is also a guy who once said the internet wouldn’t catch on back in 2000. He may have gotten that one wrong, but he’s betting on AI catching on, so I think he gives us permission to play.”

Ribeiro outlined a more structured approach, describing trust as an equation built on four elements: ownership, competence, consistency and transparency. He was matter-of-fact about why asking a nervous workforce whether it wants AI doesn’t yield an accurate answer. “You never ask a barber if you need a haircut, as the answer is always yes.”

His alternative was honesty. Companies can’t promise to protect every job, but they can promise to make employees “the most prepared, trained, trusted person” if AI disrupts their role.

Funlab, where 79% of the workforce is 21 or younger, relies on peer learning. Its “AI Super Squad” convenes representatives from every department every four weeks. Wilson said early sessions simply clarified which tools were safe, because many employees’ real limitation was “just not knowing whether I am allowed to do certain things or not.”

The report’s central concept is calibrated trust. People need to know when to rely on AI, when to verify its outputs, and when a human must decide. Blindly trusting these systems and their outputs is a significant risk.

During the Q&A, I asked how companies protect against over-trust, especially in high-intensity jobs where people just take the answer and move on. Tosky was candid. “The AI slop. It’s real,” she said. “You ask the employee a question, prompt the AI system and then they send a report without looking at it, and it’s completely wrong. It’s 10 pages you now have to read.”

Elmo keeps a human in the loop on nearly everything, and she argued that the fix starts with redesigning the work. “It’s very unsexy, but start with the process itself, instead of just going, ‘OK, let’s throw a bunch of agents at it.'”

The report recommends that IT leaders adopt a specific practice: Stop treating log-ins as a proxy for trust, and track how often people challenge or override AI outputs. Usage shows people are clicking. Override rates show they’re thinking.

I also raised a contact center concern. AI automates the mundane tasks that served as cognitive breaks for agents, leaving them with nonstop, high-intensity work and higher churn. Tosky called it “AI brain fry” and suggested rethinking metrics and breaks. Wilson added that if AI absorbs routine work, employees lose the repetition that builds context and expertise. That’s a talent pipeline problem few companies are considering.

AI that drafts content is one thing; agents that act are another. Locke said Flight Centre now has agents handling a small subset of airline ticketing that was previously outsourced offshore, with security engaged from day one. He used AI to book his Uber to the event, but a return flight to Europe? “Not yet.”

Fewer than half of respondents are very or extremely confident that their foundations are ready for more autonomous AI, and more than half say their infrastructure needs upgrading. Cisco’s 2026 Relentless Defense report found that only 36% of Australian organizations apply consistent controls to AI agents and nonhuman identities. In the report, Lendi Group CTO Devesh Maheshwari described the target as “bounded autonomy, where the agent can act on your behalf but cannot go beyond the boundaries you have established.”

This is where Cisco can help its enterprise customers. Solder argues that trust must be enforced at the network and security layers. “Built into the network and security underneath, control stops being the brake and becomes the permission to move faster,” he said. Cisco is betting that its networking, security and Splunk portfolio will become the trust layer for agentic AI, and the report provides a business rationale for that bet.

As I stated above, the research is qualitative and aligns with what I hear from CIOs globally. My advice for IT leaders:

The AI winners won’t necessarily have the best models. They’ll have employees, boards and customers who trust the systems enough to let them do more. As Solder put it, “The leaders in our research aren’t scaling AI first. They’re scaling trust.”

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#5711. Next-Gen Anticoagulant Lands FDA Nod for Secondary Stroke Prevention

— First-in-class factor XIa inhibitor was supported by the OCEANIC-Stroke trial

The FDA approved asundexian (Sunharbo) as the first factor XIa (FXIa) inhibitor for secondary stroke prevention, the agency announced on Monday.

Asundexian, an oral, direct, small-molecule inhibitor of FXIa, is indicated for use in combination with antiplatelet therapy to reduce the risk of stroke in adults following a recent mild-to-moderate non-cardioembolic ischemic stroke or a high-risk transient ischemic attack. Its selective mechanism of action is associated with a lower risk of complications compared with available anticoagulants.

"Stroke is a leading cause of disability and death in the United States, and survivors are at risk of having another stroke," said Hylton Joffe, MD, MMSc, director of the Office of Cardiology, Hematology, Endocrinology, and Nephrology in the FDA's Center for Drug Evaluation and Research, in the FDA's press release. "Today's approval represents a meaningful advance for patients and healthcare providers seeking a new option for secondary stroke prevention."

The approval was backed by the large phase III OCEANIC-Stroke trial in which treatment with asundexian led to a 26% relative reduction in the incidence of ischemic stroke through 780 days compared with placebo (6.2% vs 8.4%, HR 0.74, 95% CI 0.65-0.84).

Importantly, there was no significant increase in major bleeding risk among asundexian recipients who were on a 50-mg once-daily dose (1.9% vs 1.7% with placebo, HR 1.10, 95% CI 0.85-1.44).

Of note, asundexian is not approved for stroke prevention in people with atrial fibrillation (Afib). The FXIa inhibitor failed among Afib patients in the phase III OCEANIC-AF trial, which was stopped early for lack of efficacy.

Asundexian is not to be used concomitantly with combined P-glycoprotein and strong CYP3A4 inducers (e.g., carbamazepine, rifampin, St. John's Wort), as they may decrease its effectiveness.

Asundexian is not recommended in patients with moderate or severe hepatic impairment. It should also be withheld for at least 24 hours before an invasive procedure and for at least 24 hours after thrombolysis for acute ischemic stroke, the FDA noted.

Another FXIa inhibitor, milvexian, remains under investigation for secondary stroke prevention.

#5710. Scientists discover why chronic back pain feels so personal

For people living with chronic back pain, even a simple movement can trigger a sudden surge of pain. Now, scientists have discovered that these painful episodes activate a surprising part of the brain, one closely connected to our sense of identity and how we think about ourselves.

Researchers at UC San Diego School of Medicine found that movement-triggered pain in people with chronic low back pain (cLBP) activates a brain network that normally becomes less active during ordinary pain. The discovery suggests that persistent back pain may become deeply intertwined with a person's sense of self, potentially helping explain why conventional pain treatments often provide limited relief.

According to the World Health Organization, low back pain is the leading cause of disability worldwide. When pain persists for more than 12 weeks, it is considered chronic. For many patients, everyday movements can provoke sudden flare-ups that make an already difficult condition even harder to manage.

Although the brain plays a central role in how pain is experienced, researchers have struggled to identify the precise brain circuits responsible for pain triggered by movement.

Chronic Back Pain Activates the Brain's Sense of Self

The new study, published on October 5, 2026, in the British Journal of Anaesthesia, identified an unexpected response involving the brain's Default Mode Network (DMN).

Sometimes called the "self network," the DMN consists of interconnected regions in the frontal, parietal, and temporal lobes. These areas are especially active when our attention turns inward, such as when we reflect on personal experiences, think about our identity, or consider our thoughts and emotions. In contrast, the network generally becomes less active when we direct our attention toward something happening around us.

The researchers discovered that sudden back pain caused by movement switched this network on rather than off. This unusual response suggests that chronic pain involves more than the processing of physical sensations. It may also engage the brain systems that shape how people experience themselves.

The findings could help researchers understand why treatments that focus primarily on suppressing pain symptoms do not always work well for chronic low back pain. They also raise the possibility that targeting the DMN could offer a different approach to treatment.

Brain Scans Reveal a Surprising Difference Between Chronic and Acute Pain

To investigate what happens in the brain during a pain flare, the researchers recruited 114 patients with chronic low back pain.

Each participant completed a "leg raise test," a standard clinical procedure used to provoke back pain. During the test, researchers monitored changes in brain blood flow using a specialized functional MRI method called arterial spin labeling. This technique allows scientists to track patterns of brain activity by measuring blood flow without relying on an injected contrast agent.

The team also examined how participants responded to a separate painful stimulus. They applied a harmless but uncomfortable heat sensation to the calf, similar to the brief pain someone might experience when accidentally touching a hot stove.

Comparing these two situations revealed a striking difference.

When movement triggered a flare of chronic back pain, the DMN became more active. However, when participants experienced the painful heat stimulus, the same network became less active, following the brain's typical response to acute pain.

The researchers also identified several other important patterns:

Together, these findings provide new evidence that chronic pain flares involve brain processes associated with personal identity, not just the physical experience of pain.

Why the Brain Reacts Differently to Chronic Pain

During ordinary acute pain, the brain generally reduces activity in the DMN so it can concentrate on the immediate source of danger. This response helps shift attention away from internal thoughts and toward an external threat.

But the UC San Diego researchers found that movement triggered chronic back pain produced the opposite effect.

"In every pain study, when you're experiencing pain, the DMN deactivates," said corresponding author Fadel Zeidan, PhD, professor in the Department of Anesthesiology, endowed professor at the Sanford Institute for Empathy and Compassion, and director of the Pain Health and Mindfulness Laboratory at UC San Diego School of Medicine. "What we show for the first time ever is that when you have a pain flare, it turns on instead. You start to identify the experience with who you are."

The findings suggest that chronic back pain can become closely connected with the brain's internal representation of the self. Rather than processing pain solely as a physical warning signal, the brain may also link it to personal memories, expectations, and emotional experiences.

For someone living with chronic pain, this means the experience can extend far beyond the moments when the pain is physically present. Worry about the next flare, memories of previous episodes, and fear of movements that might trigger pain can all become part of everyday life.

"The moment-to-moment experience is contaminated not only by the feeling of pain, but by the anticipation of it and recovery from it. It's contaminated by past experiences like embarrassment about not being able to participate in normal activities and fear of movement when trying to avoid the pain."

This connection between pain and personal identity may help explain why chronic back pain can be especially difficult to treat.

A New Direction for Chronic Back Pain Treatment

Because movement-triggered chronic back pain engages different brain networks from ordinary acute pain, researchers believe traditional treatments may fail to address some of the processes that sustain the experience of chronic pain.

Medications such as opiates primarily target pain signaling, but they may not adequately address the brain networks involved in the emotional and personal dimensions of persistent pain.

"Current pain medicine is fixated on ridding patients of their pain symptoms, but that's not the source of chronic pain. These data suggest that a chronic pain flare also encompasses one's identity."

The discovery points toward treatments that address not only the sensation of pain but also the brain's relationship with that sensation.

Recent work by Zeidan and his colleagues has explored two potential approaches: mindfulness meditation and the psychedelic compound psilocybin.

Both approaches are being investigated for their ability to help people experience physical pain without allowing it to become as closely tied to their identity. Early findings suggest that changing this relationship may reduce pain intensity, although additional research is needed to confirm the results and determine how effective these treatments may be.

"These types of mind-body and psychedelic medicine approaches target the whole person," Zeidan said. "Mindfulness is a meditation technique that's about cultivating non-judgmental awareness of the present moment that dramatically reduces pain in a very unique way. Psilocybin seemingly resets the pain system that integrates trauma, past experiences and future worries to facilitate a restart, if you will. They're not a silver bullet -- you're not necessarily getting rid of the pain, but you're changing the relationship you have with that pain so it doesn't contaminate your everyday life."

Can Mindfulness and Psychedelics Change How the Brain Experiences Pain?

Rather than attempting to eliminate every pain signal, these approaches aim to change how the brain interprets and responds to the experience.

Mindfulness meditation encourages people to observe their thoughts, emotions, and physical sensations without immediately judging or reacting to them. Psilocybin, meanwhile, is being studied for its potential to alter brain processes that connect pain with earlier experiences, emotional distress, and expectations about the future.

The goal is not necessarily to remove pain altogether, but to reduce how much it influences a person's thoughts, emotions, and daily functioning.

Zeidan's laboratory is currently conducting several clinical trials using brain imaging to investigate whether mindfulness meditation and psychedelic treatments can change the neural processes involved in self-reflection. Researchers hope to determine whether these approaches can reshape brain activity and improve how people subjectively experience chronic pain.

Although the research remains at an early stage, the findings offer a different way to think about persistent back pain. Understanding why the brain connects chronic pain with a person's sense of self could eventually help scientists develop treatments that address aspects of pain that conventional therapies often miss.

Additional study authors from UC San Diego School of Medicine include Morgan Gianola, Jon Dean, Conan Chen, Daniel Barrows, Gabriel Reigner, and Thomas Liu.

Funding was provided in part by the National Institutes of Health's National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (Grant #R01AT009693) and the UC San Diego Sanford Institute for Empathy and Compassion. The researchers reported no conflicts of interest.

#5709. CMS makes it official, codifying Medicare drug price negotiations established under IRA

CMS makes it official, codifying Medicare drug price negotiations established under IRA" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Against a backdrop of repeated industry challenges in court, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) is locking in the drug price negotiation framework established under the Biden-era Inflation Reduction Act (IRA).

In turn, the process under which CMS selects certain high-spend Medicare Part B or Part D drugs and negotiates lower prices with manufacturers will carry on into 2029 and beyond. The rule codifies and expands policies previously established through guidance for the initial 2026-28 period.

The final rule is slated to go into effect Dec. 5, CMS said in a fact sheet accompanying Thursday’s announcement. By Feb. 1 of next year, CMS will select up to 20 drugs covered under Medicare Part B or Part D for price negotiations taking effect in 2029, with the potential to also select medicines included in previous rounds for renegotiation.

That upcoming group of drugs will make up the fourth cycle of pricing negotiations, with negotiated prices taking effect in 2029. CMS asserted that the rule gives both patients and drugmakers “a clear path forward as the agency builds on the program’s results and continues negotiating prices for high-cost drugs.”

The initial rounds of price negotiations have already included a slew of prominent brands, including Novo's semaglutide franchise of Wegovy and Ozempic and cancer meds like Bristol Myers Squibb’s Pomalyst, Pfizer’s Ibrance and AstraZeneca’s Calquence.

Meanwhile, the latest tranche of drugs selected earlier this year for negotiation, whose new prices would go into effect in 2028, includes notable entrants like Gilead’s HIV treatment Biktarvy, AbbVie’s Botox and Eli Lilly’s diabetes drug Trulicity, to name just a few.

Beyond codifying the framework for price negotiations in 2029 and subsequent years, CMS has also taken steps to fine-tune several elements of the program.

Namely, the rule finalizes a policy on how CMS classifies certain fixed-combination drugs, with the aim of addressing “potential program integrity concerns” that could encourage drugmakers to evade negotiated prices by steering patients toward new product formulations.

The rule also includes a provision establishing a temporary “small biotech floor” that prevents CMS from offering or accepting a counteroffer below a specified price floor for certain eligible small biotech drugs in 2029 and 2030. It also codifies two policies related to Medicare Part D intended to ensure plan coverage of medicines with a maximum fair price in effect and limit the prices plans pay pharmacies and other dispensing entities.

The IRA and the Medicare price negotiations it empowered have been frequent targets of the biopharma industry, which has broadly alleged that the policy is unconstitutional and that the pricing talks aren’t as voluntary as advertised. But attempts by major drugmakers and powerful trade organizations like the Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America (PhRMA) to push back on Medicare price negotiations have repeatedly stalled out.

In the interim, the U.S. government has made a separate and more recent push to rein in high prescription drug costs by leaning on President Donald Trump’s “most favored nation” (MFN) strategy.

“President Trump directed us to lower drug costs for Americans using every tool at our disposal,” CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz, M.D., said in a statement announcing the new rule. “This rule provides additional tools to help CMS negotiate better deals, achieve greater savings for taxpayers and beneficiaries, and improve health outcomes for seniors who rely on the Medicare Prescription Drug Program.”

MFN, for its part, has yielded at times, controversial deals with more than two dozen drugmakers, generally involving commitments to price new medicines in line with prices in high-income comparator countries and offer MFN pricing on certain existing drugs through Medicaid.

Through those deals, which have also included investment commitments in the U.S., drugmakers have been able to secure temporary exemptions from the Trump administration’s threatened pharmaceutical import tariffs.

Around this week’s midterm elections, several Big Pharma executives have signaled that they expect little immediate change to their thinking around MFN. Nevertheless, the lack of transparency surrounding the deals has already drawn scrutiny from Democratic lawmakers. With Democrats set to control both chambers of Congress beginning in January, the party may soon press harder to uncover the details of those agreements.

#5708. ADA Publications Chief Resigns

— The plan for the organization's key journal amid the ongoing boycott is a concern, he says

The vice president of publications at the American Diabetes Association (ADA) has resigned amid the ongoing boycott of the organization.

Christian Kohler, who was with the ADA for 22 years, expressed "profound disappointment" at the overall handling of events at this year's annual meeting in New Orleans, but said in his resignation letter that his "immediate decision" to leave was tied to what's happening at the ADA's flagship journal Diabetes Care.

That includes ADA attempting to bring in interim editors while the majority of the journal's staff participates in the boycott.

"Throughout my nearly three decades in scientific and medical publishing, I have worked to uphold the principles of editorial independence, scientific integrity, transparency, and accountability," Kohler wrote. "Based on that experience, I believe the proposed interim editorial arrangement presents serious ethical, operational, and reputational risks."

In particular, Kohler said he's concerned about how interim staff brought in during the boycott have to perform their duties without an editor in chief who assumes ultimate responsibility for everything in the journal. The absence of a formal process to evaluate interim editors' "suitability for handling the breadth and complexity of research" submitted to the journal is also "problematic," he noted in his letter.

He said he also believes these interim editors are "being placed in an untenable position, one in which their ability to succeed will be severely constrained by circumstances beyond their control, potentially placing their own professional reputations at risk."

The approach to bring in interim editors won't restore confidence in the publication, Kohler added.

"To be clear, I fear it will further undermine the credibility, integrity, and international reputation of Diabetes Care, a journal whose standing has been built over decades through the contributions of dedicated editors, reviewers, authors, and ADA publications staff," he wrote.

In an emailed statement to MedPage Today, the ADA defended its actions on Diabetes Care, noting that its interim editorial board consists of "highly experienced and respected healthcare professionals who have dedicated their careers to caring for people living with diabetes, including endocrinologists, primary care physicians focused on diabetes care, diabetes educators, and more."

ADA added that it is in "conversations with some of the people leading the boycott to schedule a meeting," and that it previously outlined the "next steps that we plan to take to learn and improve based on the facts that came to bear from the review."

Many have criticized the organization's final report on what happened at the annual meeting, taking issue with what it described as perceived threats to "disrupt and protest" the event. That final report also said ADA members who were kicked out of the meeting did not violate its code of conduct, a reversal from an earlier version of the report.

The ADA has lost several leaders in the wake of the annual meeting; Chief Science and Medical Officer Rita Kalyani, MD, and ADA Board Chair James Tai left just before the final report came out. Other resignations came soon after the five researchers were booted from the meeting, including Scientific Sessions Planning Committee Chair Mark Atkinson, PhD, and President-Elect Jennifer Green, MD.

Kohler also said the ADA hasn't yet meaningfully addressed the concerns raised by more than 1,200 people participating in the boycott, which launched in September.

"This is not a frivolous exercise for the boycotters," Kohler told MedPage Today, noting that many of them have spent decades volunteering for ADA programs.

"These are the people ... that ADA leadership should be engaging with most closely to confront the challenges faced by people with diabetes and the scientific and medical communities," he said. "That's not happening."

As the ADA "tries to outrun this storm," he added, it's "missing an opportunity to work with and support the professional community on so many urgent, critical issues."

"My sincere hope is that my letter will play some small role in facilitating a discussion and real action that resolves the boycott," he noted. "I, too, invested a lot in the organization over the years, and I also care deeply about its mission."

Kohler said his resignation would be effective Nov. 30.

#5707. Less than 42 minutes of bright daylight linked to higher dementia risk

Could the amount of daylight you get each day offer clues about your risk of developing dementia? A large new study suggests that exposure to brighter daytime light is associated with a lower likelihood of developing the condition.

The findings, published in General Psychiatry, point to daytime light exposure as a potentially overlooked factor in brain health.

Brighter Daylight Linked to Lower Dementia Risk

To investigate the connection, researchers analyzed data from 87,577 adults who wore wrist devices equipped with accelerometers. The devices allowed scientists to measure participants' exposure to light during both the day and night. Over a median follow-up period of 8.1 years, 741 participants developed dementia.

The results revealed a notable pattern. People exposed to average daytime light levels exceeding 1,000 lux (a moderately bright light level equivalent to an overcast day outdoors) had a 16% lower risk of developing dementia. Spending longer periods in even brighter daytime light (at least 5,000 lux) was associated with further reductions in risk.

Too Little Daylight Emerges as a Surprising Dementia Risk Indicator

One of the most striking findings involved people who received very little bright light during the day. Getting less than 0.7 hours, or 42 minutes, of bright daytime light daily was a stronger predictor of dementia than 6 established dementia risk factors.

Interestingly, researchers found no statistically significant connection between nighttime light exposure and dementia risk. This suggests that daytime brightness, rather than light exposure at night, may be particularly relevant to the relationship identified in the study.

"Daytime light exposure may serve as a novel indicator of dementia risk," said corresponding author Hongliang Feng, PhD, of Guangzhou Medical University, in China.

Although the findings reveal an association, they do not establish that getting more daylight directly prevents dementia. Instead, the research highlights daytime light exposure as a potentially valuable indicator of dementia risk that deserves further investigation.

#5706. Hims & Hers inks deal with Eli Lilly to offer branded weight loss drugs

Hims & Hers inks deal with Eli Lilly to offer branded weight loss drugs" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Hims & Hers struck a deal with Eli Lilly to offer the drugmaker’s branded obesity treatments through its online health and wellness platform.

Under the agreement, Eli Lilly will give Hims & Hers pharmacies direct access to its U.S. Food and Drug Administration-approved GLP-1 medications at self-pay prices. Eligible patients on the Hims & Hers platform can be prescribed and order Eli Lilly's injectable Zepbound (tirzepatide) and daily oral medication Foundayo (orforglipron) without leaving the company's platform.

Prior to this agreement, Lilly drugs were available to patients on Hims & Hers only if they left the site and went to Lilly's direct-to-consumer platform, LillyDirect.

Shares of Hims & Hers jumped 8% Friday following news of the Eli Lilly partnership.

The agreement brings together Lilly’s obesity medicines and Hims & Hers’ consumer platform to expand consumers' access to FDA-approved weight loss drugs, the companies said.

"Patients can complete a consultation, receive a prescription if their provider determines it is appropriate and have an FDA-approved Lilly medicine shipped directly to their home, all in one seamless experience," the companies said in a press release.

Self-pay pricing starts at $149 per month for Foundayo and $299 per month for Zepbound.

"At Lilly, we are always looking for new ways to help more people get the medicines they need, and that means meeting patients where they already are," said Ilya Yuffa, executive vice president and president, Lilly USA and global customer capabilities, Eli Lilly and Company, in a statement. "Millions of people turn to Hims & Hers for their care, and through this agreement, those patients now have a simple, more direct way to get FDA-approved Lilly medicine at an affordable price if prescribed."

Hims & Hers' technology platform supports provider outreach, follow-up care and treatment planning. Weight loss patients on Hims & Hers receive a membership experience that includes 24/7 access to a care team, nutrition guidance, regular clinical check-ins and access to the Hims & Hers Weight Loss community, according to the company.

The agreement with Eli Lilly mirrors Hims & Hers' partnership with Novo Nordisk, which has been selling its branded weight loss drugs Wegovy and Ozempic through Hims & Hers since March. Novo had previously sued the telehealth company for offering compounded versions of its medications. Hims & Hers' agreement with Novo marked a shift in its obesity strategy toward FDA-approved branded GLP-1 treatments and away from cheaper compounded GLP-1 drugs.

Earlier this year, Hims & Hers took heat from the pharmaceutical manufacturer and federal regulators after announcing plans to launch a knockoff of Novo's oral pill. It backed down from those plans under pressure.

Hims & Hers stated that it never offered access to compounded copies of Lilly’s GLP-1 drugs and has committed not to do so in the future.

As part of the agreement, the companies have committed to protecting independent clinical decision-making, so that providers on the Hims & Hers platform continue to prescribe the treatment they determine is right for each patient.

“Lilly is one of the most innovative pharmaceutical companies in history, and I’m incredibly proud that Hims & Hers is a part of making sure more people can access the medicines they’ve created,” said Andrew Dudum, co-founder and CEO of Hims & Hers, in a statement. “By working together, we’re not just reaching more people with obesity with seamless, personal access to FDA-approved Lilly medicine. We’re showing the industry what innovators can achieve for customers everywhere when we work together to make the world well.”

Hims & Hers has faced financial pressure as it shifts from high-margin compounded GLP-1s to lower-margin branded weight-loss drugs. The company posted a $92 million loss in Q1, including $33 million in restructuring costs, largely from write-downs of its compounded GLP-1 supply chain, which executives said faced “risk of obsolescence.”

In Q2, Hims & Hers reported an $86 million loss, compared with a $43 million profit a year earlier. The quarter included $81 million in one-time costs, including expenses tied to its exit from compounded GLP-1s.

#5705. Another Option for Rare Benign Soft-Tissue Tumor Wins FDA Approval

— Pimicotinib achieved 54% objective response rate in unresectable tenosynovial giant cell tumor

The FDA approved the small-molecule inhibitor pimicotinib (Pimjetmi) for selected patients with symptomatic tenosynovial giant cell tumor (TGCT) and high surgical risk.

An oral selective inhibitor of colony stimulating factor-1 receptor (CSF-1R), pimicotinib is indicated for TGCT for which surgery might cause worsening functional limitation or severe morbidity. Pimicotinib is the third FDA-approved drug for TGCT, joining two other CSF-1R inhibitors, vimseltinib (Romvimza), approved in 2025, and pexidartinib (Turalio), approved in 2019.

TGCT is a rare, locally aggressive soft-tissue tumor that primarily affects otherwise healthy younger (median age 38) adults. The condition originates in the joint synovium, bursae, or tendon sheaths and has the potential to cause substantial functional limitation and morbidity. Surgery is the primary treatment when feasible.

Primary support for the approval came from the phase III MANEUVER trial. Investigators in Asia, Europe, and North America randomized 94 patients with unresectable TGCT 2:1 to pimicotinib or placebo. The trial met the primary endpoint of objective response rate (ORR) at week 25. The primary analysis showed an ORR of 54% with pimicotinib and 3% with placebo (P<0.0001).

Recently reported 2-year results from the trial showed durable responses with pimicotinib (76-78% at 2 years), along with improvements in pain, stiffness, and range of motion.

"For people living with TGCT, the impact of the disease is often felt through persistent limitations in mobility, physical function, and the ability to carry out everyday activities," investigator Vinod Ravi, MD, of the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center in Houston, said last month in a press release from drugmaker EMD Serono announcing those results.

"What is encouraging about these 2-year findings is the consistency of improvements, not only in the durability of tumor response, but across the symptoms and functional outcomes that matter to patients," added Ravi. "Together with the observed safety profile, these results provide important insight into the potential for pimicotinib to deliver meaningful benefit over time."

According to the FDA, the most common adverse reactions in the pimicotinib arm (>20% of patients) were pruritus, rash, facial and periorbital edema, fatigue, nausea, headache, and peripheral edema. Laboratory abnormalities occurring in more than 30% of patients consisted of increased creatine phosphokinase, lactate dehydrogenase, aspartate aminotransferase, lipase, cholesterol, amylase, and alanine aminotransferase.

Pimicotinib was approved earlier this year in Canada and Switzerland and in China in 2025.

Weekly Rundown: Hims & Hers adds new partners for benefits program; Hippocratic unveils updates to healthcare-focused AI model" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Stay up to date on the latest in health tech, digital health and health AI news with this weekly brief. Read below for news from the week of Nov. 2 to 6.

Hims & Hers announced Thursday the addition of four new partners to its benefits program, bringing the total of included partners to 14.

The new partners are nutrition gummy maker Grüns; air medical transport membership service Medjet; AI-powered home strength system Tonal and full body intelligence provider Viome.

Superscript is opening access to its platform through the launch of a new API, which allows any healthcare practice or electronic health record system to access real-time healthcare pricing information.

The platform, backed by Mark Cuban and Nava Ventures, is currently live with 1,500 active healthcare providers.  To date, it has served more than 500,000 patients and processed 2.2 million patient billing transactions, executives say.

One of the organizations Superscript works with is Michigan-based Orthopaedic Associates of Muskegon (OAM).

“Patients deserve certainty not only in their clinical diagnosis and treatment plans, but also in their financial obligations,” said Jeff Cave, OAM CEO, in a statement. “Historically, doctors and administrative teams had no way of knowing exact insurance reimbursement rates at the point of care. Partnering with Superscript lets our patients know exactly what they owe before their visit. That transparency builds trust, eliminates anxiety, and allows our care team to focus entirely on delivering high-quality care.”

Hippocratic AI launched Monday a new generation of its healthcare language model that features six new upgrades to its AI agents.

The company says the new version of its healthcare-focused AI model can conduct more natural and responsive patient conversations by interpreting emotional cues, reasoning while speaking and adapting its voice in real time, while improving safety, speed and electronic health record system integration.

The upgrade—dubbed Polaris 6 Ultra—features what executives call “bedside intuition,” a first-of-its-kind capability that reads patients’ emotional state and decides next speech without pause.

“In healthcare, you don't get credit for reminding a patient. You get credit for the action they take,” said Munjal Shah, Hippocratic AI CEO and co-founder, in a statement. “Polaris 6.0 was built from more than 323 million patient conversations, making it the only truly experienced frontier model for healthcare able to operate safely and autonomously to drive patient outcomes. That experience shows. Polaris 6.0 handles the healthcare edge cases of real life, it now has more human-like common sense and pacing, and it delivers the kind of empathy that persuades patients.”

Other capabilities include AI intuition, an upgraded version of Care Voice and enhanced Common Sense.

Polaris 6 Ultra also runs on 7.4 trillion parameters and delivers a 1.3X end-to-end speedup compared to Polaris 5, the company says.

A coalition of organizations is calling on the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) to extend its telemedicine prescribing flexibilities deadline given the lack of finalization to a key rule.

The flexibilities are set to expire on Dec. 31, and the agency’s Special Registrations for Telemedicine and Limited State Telemedicine Registrations final rule has not been published.

The coalition said patients and providers are “facing unacceptable uncertainty and the real risk of care disruptions,” noting that providers and platforms will need time to review requirements and apply for registration even if the rule is published in November.

“Patients should not have to wonder in December whether their January appointments will happen—or whether they will lose access to medications they rely on,” said Chris Adamec, Alliance for Connected Care executive director, in a statement. “With 59 days remaining and no published final rule, DEA can give providers and patients the stability they need by issuing a fifth extension as soon as possible.”

Advocates are calling for an extension through at least Dec. 31, 2027.
