#5703. Alphabet’s Wing to invest $125M in new delivery drone factory

Wing Aviation LLC today announced plans to spend $125 million on the construction of a new delivery drone factory.

The initiative is part of a broader investment that also encompasses the Alphabet Inc. unit’s research and development teams in California. Additionally, Wing stated that it plans to invest in the communities where it operates. It currently offers deliveries in five U.S. cities and intends to bring its service to 14 more markets soon.

Wing is building its factory in Fort Worth, Texas. The 15,000-square-foot facility is expected to create up to 100 jobs. Wing says it will have capacity to make tens of thousands of delivery drones per year, which should significantly speed up its market expansion efforts.

The Alphabet unit’s drones reportedly have a wingspan of about 4.9 feet. They’re based on a frame made of styrofoam, a foam that mostly consists of trapped air, and carbon fibers. Styrofoam is lightweight and repels water, which comes handy when a drone is navigating challenging weather. The frame’s carbon fibers, in turn, boost its sturdiness.

The drone frame is equipped with 16 electric rotors that enable it to reach speeds of up to 60 miles per hour. Workers at stores that use Wing’s delivery service attach merchandise to its drones via a tether. After a drone takes off, it reels in the tether until the package comes into physical contact with its frame. When it reaches the customer’s house, the drone descends to an altitude of 20 feet and lowers the parcel.

Wing has built a software stack that automates much of the work involved in coordinating deliveries. It picks the most suitable drone for a given delivery run, plans its flight path and ensures that it won’t interfere with other drones. Human safety teams monitor for weather and air traffic changes that may make it necessary to adjust flight plans.

The unit plans to make its delivery service available to more than 40 million Americans by 2027. It’s pursuing the growth initiative in partnership with retailers such as Walmart Inc., which uses its drones to process e-commerce purchases. Last month, the latter company announced plans to make Wing deliveries available at more than 270 stores.

The Alphabet unit also intends to offer its service in Japan. Last month, it teamed up with Tokyo-based internet provider KDDI Corp. to make drone deliveries available to local consumers in 2027.

Although the drone delivery market is in an early stage, Wing already faces a significant amount of competition. In August, Amazon.com Inc. announced plans to make its Prime Air service available in nearly 500 U.S. markets by year’s end. More recently, drone delivery startup Zipline International Inc. raised $1.5 billion in funding at a $21.5 billion valuation.

#5702. Why some “lower-risk” childhood cancers turn deadly

Some childhood cancers may be far more dangerous than their initial risk classification suggests. Scientists have discovered that certain tumors considered less threatening can contain hidden populations of highly aggressive cancer cells, potentially explaining why some children experience devastating outcomes despite lacking the usual genetic warning signs.

The discovery could change how doctors identify children at risk of life-threatening cancer, allowing treatment to be better matched to the true aggressiveness of their disease.

The findings, published in Cancer Research, come from scientists at the Wellcome Sanger Institute, the University of Cambridge, Great Ormond Street Hospital (GOSH), University College London, and collaborating institutions. Their research focused on rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS), an aggressive cancer that develops from muscle tissue and is among the most common soft tissue cancers affecting children younger than 15. Approximately 55 children are diagnosed with the disease in the United Kingdom each year.[1]

Unlike many adult cancers, which can develop after years of aging or exposure to environmental factors, childhood cancers often result from genetic changes that occur during early development.

Why Some Childhood Cancers Defy Risk Predictions

Doctors generally divide rhabdomyosarcoma into two main categories based on whether a tumor carries a particular genetic warning sign. This marker occurs when two genes that are normally separate become fused together, creating an abnormal genetic combination associated with especially aggressive disease.[2]

Children whose tumors contain this fusion have substantially lower survival rates than those without it, even when they receive intensive treatment.

But this classification has a troubling limitation. Some children whose tumors lack the high-risk genetic marker still develop aggressive cancers that can prove fatal. Until now, scientists have struggled to explain why these supposedly less dangerous tumors sometimes behave so aggressively.

To investigate this mystery, the research team compared tumors from children with different forms of rhabdomyosarcoma, looking beyond the genetic markers traditionally used to estimate risk.

The researchers examined tumor samples from 16 children, including four whose cancers lacked the fusion marker but proved fatal, four with fusion-positive tumors, and eight children with fusion-negative disease who remained alive.

Using advanced genetic analysis, scientists studied the tumors at a level of detail that conventional techniques cannot easily achieve.

One of their main tools was single-cell RNA sequencing, a technology that measures gene activity in individual cells. Rather than examining a tumor as a single mass, this approach allows researchers to investigate the behavior of its different cell populations and identify potentially dangerous cells that might otherwise go unnoticed.

The scientists also used spatial transcriptomics, a technique that maps gene activity to specific locations within a tumor. This provided a clearer picture of where aggressive cancer cells were concentrated and how they were distributed throughout the tissue.

The results revealed a striking similarity between tumors that had previously been placed in different risk categories. Some cancers classified as non-high-risk contained cells with gene activity patterns closely resembling those found in high-risk tumors.

Even more surprisingly, these aggressive tumors did not need the same genetic mutations to produce similar behavior. Researchers identified rare genetic changes that affected many of the same cellular pathways involved in the most dangerous forms of the disease.

This suggests that different genetic abnormalities can ultimately push cancer cells toward a shared aggressive state. In other words, tumors can reach a similarly dangerous biological condition through multiple genetic routes, even when they lack the warning sign typically used to identify high-risk disease.

Dr. Karin Straathof, co-senior author at UCL Cancer Institute and GOSH, said:

"By studying tumors one cell at a time, we uncovered hidden populations of aggressive cancer cells that conventional methods miss. Although these tumors carry different genetic changes, many converge on the same aggressive pathways. This helps explain why some children who appear to have lower-risk disease can still have a devastating outcome."

A New Path Toward More Precise Cancer Treatment

The findings could have important implications for how childhood cancer is diagnosed and treated.

If doctors can identify the distinctive biological signatures of aggressive cancer cells at diagnosis, they may be able to recognize children who face a greater risk of relapse or death, even when standard genetic tests suggest otherwise.

Such an approach could also help prevent unnecessary treatment. Children with genuinely lower-risk tumors might avoid some of the harmful side effects associated with intensive chemotherapy, while those with hidden aggressive disease could receive stronger or more targeted treatment earlier.

The researchers are particularly interested in identifying markers that could be used to develop therapies aimed specifically at the most dangerous cancer cells.

One possible direction involves immunotherapy, including CAR-T cell therapy. This treatment uses specially modified immune cells to recognize and attack cancer cells. Although such treatments would require further development and testing for rhabdomyosarcoma, they could eventually offer a more precise alternative to conventional chemotherapy, potentially reducing damage to healthy tissues.

Scientists are now expanding their research to include hundreds of additional tumor samples. By studying a much larger group of patients, they hope to uncover more of the rare genetic changes capable of producing aggressive cancer and accelerate the development of personalized treatments.

Sara Wakeling, Chief Executive Officer and co-founder of Alice's Arc, said:

"Every child with cancer deserves the best possible chance of survival. We're proud to support research into rhabdomyosarcoma, showing how cutting-edge technologies can uncover the biology driving aggressive childhood cancers. These discoveries bring us closer to more personalized treatments and better outcomes for children."

Dr. Laura Danielson, Children's and Young Person's Lead at Cancer Research UK, said:

"Discovery research like this is essential to understand the unique biology of these cancers. This important study demonstrates that aggressive tumors may share similar features, even if they carry different genetic changes. By helping researchers understand what these high-risk cancers have in common, this work adds a vital piece to the puzzle and could help guide future efforts to improve treatment for children and young people with rhabdomyosarcoma."

Rethinking How Doctors Identify Dangerous Childhood Cancers

Beyond its potential treatment applications, the discovery challenges a fundamental assumption about how rhabdomyosarcoma should be classified.

Instead of viewing aggressive disease primarily through the presence or absence of one genetic abnormality, the researchers suggest that doctors may need to consider the broader biological state of the cancer cells themselves.

This distinction is important because tumors with different mutations can behave in remarkably similar ways. Identifying the shared features of aggressive disease could provide a more reliable way to recognize children who need intensive treatment, regardless of the particular genetic changes driving their tumors.

Professor Sam Behjati, co-senior author formerly at the Wellcome Sanger Institute and Head of the Department of Paediatrics at the University of Cambridge, said:

"This work changes how we think about rhabdomyosarcoma. Rather than a single, abnormal gene, we've shown that there is an overarching cell state of aggressive disease that defies conventional classification systems. Understanding this shared biology could help identify children who need more intense treatment to improve their survival."

Although further research is needed before these findings can change routine clinical care, they provide a promising foundation for more accurate risk assessments and treatments tailored to each child's cancer.

By revealing aggressive behavior hidden beneath seemingly reassuring genetic classifications, scientists hope to improve survival for children with the most dangerous tumors while sparing others from treatment they may not need.

The research received support through a Cancer Research UK -- Children with Cancer UK Innovation Award, with additional co-funding from Alice's Arc and funding from Wellcome.

#5701. Billy Joel Back on Stage; Alzheimer's and Sleep; Predicting Parkinson's Progression

— News and commentary from the world of neurology and neuroscience

Musician and songwriter Billy Joel announced his first official show since his normal pressure hydrocephalus diagnosis. (People)

Topline results from a phase II study showed that treatment with investigational PGN-EDODM1 led to improvements in multiple functional measures in patients with myotonic dystrophy type 1, drugmaker PepGen said.

Patients diagnosed with iatrogenic cerebral amyloid angiopathy had a high rate of subsequent symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage -- roughly a 20% yearly risk -- case series data showed. (Neurology)

Slow-wave sleep was linked to cognitive trajectories in preclinical Alzheimer's disease patients, with possibly stronger associations in men. (Alzheimer's Research & Therapy)

Final data from an open-label trial of the CD19-directed CAR T-cell therapy mivocabtagene autoleucel for stiff person syndrome -- first reported at this year's American Academy of Neurology (AAN) annual meeting -- were published in JAMA Neurology.

And JAMA Neurology published positive phase III trial data on azetukalner for focal seizures, which was also first reported at the AAN meeting.

In a correspondence to the New England Journal of Medicine, researchers demonstrated an initial proof of concept for chemogenetic neuromodulation in patients with drug-resistant epilepsy.

Older age, bilateral symmetric parkinsonism, and rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder at diagnosis were associated with faster Parkinson's disease progression, an Italian cohort study showed. (Journal of Neurology, Neurosurgery & Psychiatry)

Exposure to petroleum-derived lubricants in the workplace was linked with a higher risk of multiple sclerosis in a Swedish population-based case-control study. (Neurology)

In a study of people treated for overactive bladder, beta-3 agonists were not associated with a lower dementia incidence compared with anticholinergics. (JAMA Network Open)

#5700. Doximity expands clinical AI footprint to more than 190 health systems

Doximity expands clinical AI footprint to more than 190 health systems" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Doximity is rapidly expanding its clinical AI footprint with health systems, with more than 190 organizations having now purchased its AI suite, up from 165 organizations last quarter.

Those health system customers include 10 of the nation's top 20 hospitals, Doximity executives said during the company's fiscal 2027 second-quarter earnings call on Thursday.

NewYork-Presbyterian has integrated Doximity’s AI tools directly into its electronic health record (EHR) workflow. The partnership grants clinicians across NewYork-Presbyterian, Columbia University Irving Medical Center and Weill Cornell Medicine frictionless access to AI tools, including Doximity Scribe and Doximity Ask, the company's AI-powered clinical decision support tool.

NewYork-Presbyterian rolled out Doximity’s AI suite to clinicians across 10 hospitals and hundreds of locations. The deployment builds on NYP’s use of Doximity for video and phone visits since 2021.

UCSD Health is one of the first hospitals to adopt Doximity's new patient context feature, which allows AI to ingest EHR charts, labs, and patient history directly to give patient-specific answers and guideline-based treatment plans, Jeff Tangney, Doximity CEO, said during the earnings call.

"Our patient context feature is now available for thousands of doctors, and they're writing prompts half as long, 12 words versus our 24-word average, because they no longer have to retype the chart details into a search bar. Our AI already has the labs, notes, and problem list, so it can find the pertinent clinical details deep in their record," Tangney said.

The company is also opening API access to its clinical intelligence layer to expand to more workflows.

Tangney stressed that Doximity is focused on offering clinicians a full clinical AI suite across workflows including telehealth, AI documentation, scheduling, clinical questions, patient context and clinical evidence.

"We offer them a suite, not a search bar," Tangney said. "That suite allows them to do the telehealth visit, to have notes taken on that visit, what we call Scribe, and then to ask questions about that visit with the patient context."

Doximity is a digital platform for U.S. medical professionals that offers workflow tools such as a telehealth solution, a clinician-to-patient dialer tool and digital faxing capabilities. The company aims to become a leading AI platform for doctors with plans to scale its clinical AI suite, including its ambient note-taking tool Scribe and clinical AI assistant and medical search engine Ask. A year ago, Doximity acquired clinical AI company Pathway and then integrated Pathway's datasets and its AI into its free Doximity GPT product to offer DoxGPT (now Ask).

Doximity is leaning hard into AI accuracy and safety as AI adoption rapidly grows. AI accuracy "is the number one concern doctors have about AI," Tangney told investors and analysts on the call. "AI deals in probabilities. Patient care demands precision," he said.

The company is making clinical reliability a major part of its competitive positioning. Doximity recently launched DoseCheck, a deterministic verifier for medication safety. Through a partnership with Wolters Kluwer Health, the company embedded UpToDate's evidence-based clinical content directly within Doximity Ask.

"Every clinical AI model has read the National Library of Medicine, which has all of the journals and guidelines, but Wolters Kluwer's UpToDate stands alone as the proprietary gold standard reference for point of care. Their 7,600 physician authors provide unique advice about what to do when there is not an RCT, or randomized controlled trial, to answer the question," Tangney said.

The partnership with UpToDate represents a "strong synergy of Doximity's AI evidence tools and [UpToDate's] unique expert opinion and physician expertise," he noted.

UpToDate has 2,500 health systems as clients, compared to Doximity's 190, and that creates "additional synergies" for the company, Tangney said. Doximity plans to expand its relationship with UpToDate, he noted: "It's the beginning of what we think will be a very strategic, long-term partnership," he added.

Physician AI engagement is growing quickly, according to the company.  Doximity said quarterly active workflow prescribers increased 34% year over year, accelerating from the prior quarter. Approximately half of the 1.8 million U.S. prescribers, roughly 900,000 clinicians, used Doximity workflow products during the quarter. The company sees continued growth in telehealth and scheduling alongside rapidly expanding use of AI and patient-specific clinical tools, Tangney said.

A year ago, the company's workflow active-user growth was in the single digits versus 34% now, Matt Sonefeldt, Doximity's chief financial officer, said during the call. Doximity is investing heavily in AI. Rapid growth in clinician engagement, particularly with the company's workflow tools, is laying the groundwork for greater monetization and business growth over the next several years, Sonefeldt said.

Doximity reported $174.5 million in revenue during the quarter ending September 30, up 4% year over year, beating guidance. Adjusted EBITDA was $89 million, or a 51% margin, despite AI spending growing more than sixfold year over year.

The company reported net income of $34.7 million, versus $62.1 million a year ago, representing a margin of 19.9%, versus 36.8%. And the company reported adjusted EPS of 36 cents per share.

The company's Q2 results beat Wall Street analysts' estimates as analysts expected revenue of $170.8 million, adjusted EBITDA of $81 million and adjusted EPS of 35 cents per share.

Doximity raised its full-year revenue outlook to $678 million to $683 million, about 6% growth at the midpoint. For the full year, the company expects adjusted EBITDA between $317 million and $325 million.

The company launched its commercial AI Search product for pharmaceutical companies in late April, and it's gaining traction with pharmaceutical advertisers, executives said. Sixteen of the top 20 companies have purchased it, with three more in contracting, and bookings have reached eight figures, Sonefeldt said. AI Search revenue will ramp up gradually through calendar 2027, he noted.

AI monetization is coming from the pharma side and selling AI Search as an advertising product, Sonefeldt noted. "We do sell AI as a separate enterprise agreement to health systems customers. We charge a nominal amount as part of our broader workflow suite. As we think about this going forward, we see the primary monetization engine being on the pharma side of our business, specifically through the ad products that we sell," he told analysts during a Q&A on the call.

On the clinical side, Doximity aims to build a trusted AI workflow layer that physicians use for documentation, clinical questions, patient-specific decision support, telehealth and communication. On the commercial side, the company sees opportunities to turn that engagement and clinical intent into a new advertising and search business serving pharma.

"With AI Search now available to our pharma clients, we're growing into a much larger market," Tangney told analysts and investors. "We think we're entering a whole new market here, which has historically been paid search."

Doximity is trying to capture marketing dollars that historically went to Google and other search channels. Tangney cited an estimated $14 billion spent annually by pharma on paid search in the U.S.

The company also plans to introduce biddable or auction-based purchasing, which would make the product look much more like conventional paid search.

Shares of Doximity slumped following its Thursday evening earnings report as investors reacted to significant margin compression, Yahoo Finance reported. Doximity's stock is down nearly 25% this year.

"On the stock, while shares have shed roughly a quarter of value year-to-date due to lingering questions about AI threats and the uncertain backdrop for pharma marketing spend, solid results such as these, along with positive commentary around macro factors should continue to power the recovery that has been ongoing since the fiscal first-quarter earnings print," Ryan Daniels, group head of healthcare technology and services at William Blair, wrote in an analyst note.

"We continue to be optimistic on Doximity's competitive position, with robust growth in utilization metrics and novel AI offerings launching to pharma partners. Continued development of AI-based workflow solutions should support Doximity’s ability to remain a share gainer in healthcare professional (HCP) marketing, supporting long-term growth above market averages," Daniels wrote.

#5699. The Power of Schema Markup: A Comprehensive Guide for Real Estate Agents

The digital world has revolutionized how real estate is marketed and sold, placing a premium on strategic online presence and data-driven advertising. Among the myriad online tools available, Schema Markup stands out as an extremely potent weapon for real estate agents. This article offers a comprehensive look at how real estate agents can effectively use Schema Markup to bolster their online presence, increase organic reach, and drive sales.

Before discussing its application, let's first demystify what Schema Markup is. Schema Markup, also known as Structured Data, is a form of microdata. #5698. Six popular sugar substitutes linked to faster brain aging

Sugar substitutes are often promoted as a healthier way to enjoy sweet foods and drinks without consuming as much sugar. However, new research suggests that some of these widely used sweeteners may have an unexpected downside for long-term brain health.

A study published in Neurology, the medical journal of the American Academy of Neurology, found that people who consumed the most low- and no-calorie sweeteners experienced significantly faster declines in memory and thinking skills than those who consumed the least. The association was particularly pronounced among people with diabetes.

Researchers examined seven sweeteners commonly used in foods and beverages: aspartame, saccharin, acesulfame-K, erythritol, xylitol, sorbitol and tagatose. These ingredients frequently appear in ultra-processed products, including diet sodas, flavored waters, energy drinks, yogurt and low-calorie desserts. Some are also sold separately for sweetening foods and beverages.

"Low- and no-calorie sweeteners are often seen as a healthy alternative to sugar; however, our findings suggest certain sweeteners may have negative effects on brain health over time," said study author Claudia Kimie Suemoto, MD, PhD, of the University of São Paulo in Brazil.

Importantly, the findings show an association rather than a proven cause-and-effect relationship. Researchers cannot conclude from this study that consuming these sweeteners directly damages the brain or causes memory loss.

Study Tracks Nearly 13,000 Adults for Eight Years

To investigate whether sugar substitutes might be connected to cognitive health, researchers analyzed data from 12,772 adults across Brazil. Participants were 52 years old on average when the study began and were followed for approximately eight years.

At the beginning of the study, participants completed detailed dietary questionnaires describing the foods and drinks they had consumed during the previous year. Researchers used these responses to estimate each person's daily intake of the seven sweeteners.

Participants were then separated into three groups according to how much of the sweeteners they consumed. Those in the lowest consumption group averaged 20 milligrams per day (mg/day), while those in the highest group averaged 191 mg/day. For comparison, 191 milligrams of aspartame is roughly the amount found in one can of diet soda.

Of the seven sweeteners examined, sorbitol had the highest average intake, at 64 mg/day. Sorbitol belongs to a category of sweeteners called sugar alcohols, which provide sweetness and are commonly used as sugar substitutes.

Throughout the study, participants completed cognitive assessments at three points: the beginning, middle, and end. These tests measured several abilities essential for everyday mental functioning, including memory, language, and the speed at which the brain processes information.

Researchers evaluated verbal fluency, or the ability to quickly retrieve and produce words, along with working memory, which allows people to temporarily hold and use information. They also tested word recall and processing speed to determine how these abilities changed over time.

High Sweetener Consumption Linked to 62% Faster Cognitive Decline

The results revealed a striking difference between people who consumed the most sweeteners and those who consumed the least.

After accounting for factors that could influence cognitive health, including age, sex, high blood pressure, and cardiovascular disease, researchers found that participants in the highest consumption group experienced a 62% faster decline in overall thinking and memory abilities compared with those in the lowest group.

That difference was equivalent to approximately 1.6 additional years of cognitive aging over the study period.

Even moderate consumption was associated with measurable differences. Participants in the middle group experienced a 35% faster decline than those consuming the least, equivalent to roughly 1.3 additional years of cognitive aging.

These estimates describe changes in cognitive test performance rather than a direct measurement of biological brain aging. They also do not mean that everyone who consumes artificial sweeteners will experience memory problems.

Stronger Links Found in Adults Under 60 and People With Diabetes

When researchers examined different age groups, they discovered that the association was not consistent across all participants.

Among adults younger than 60, higher sweetener consumption was linked to faster declines in verbal fluency and overall cognitive performance. However, researchers did not find a similar association among participants older than 60.

The relationship was also stronger in people with diabetes than in those without the condition. This finding is especially relevant because people with diabetes frequently turn to sugar substitutes to help manage their sugar intake.

Examining the sweeteners individually revealed another important distinction. Six of the seven substances were associated with faster declines in overall cognitive performance, particularly memory.

Those six were aspartame, saccharin, acesulfame-K, erythritol, sorbitol and xylitol.

Tagatose was the exception. Researchers found no association between its consumption and cognitive decline in this study. However, that finding does not establish that tagatose protects the brain or is necessarily safer than other sweeteners.

Should People Rethink Artificial Sweeteners?

The findings raise important questions about whether replacing sugar with low-calorie alternatives always delivers the health benefits consumers expect, particularly when it comes to the brain.

"While we found links to cognitive decline for middle-aged people both with and without diabetes, people with diabetes are more likely to use artificial sweeteners as sugar substitutes," Suemoto said. "More research is needed to confirm our findings and to investigate if other refined sugar alternatives, such as applesauce, honey, maple syrup or coconut sugar, may be effective alternatives."

Researchers also acknowledged several limitations. The analysis did not cover every artificial sweetener available on the market, so the findings cannot necessarily be applied to all sugar substitutes.

In addition, dietary information came from participants' own recollections of what they had eaten and drunk. Because people may forget foods, underestimate portions, or inaccurately report their habits, these estimates may not perfectly reflect actual sweetener consumption.

The observational design also means that other factors could help explain the relationship between sweetener intake and cognitive decline, despite researchers' efforts to account for several important health differences.

Further studies will be needed to determine whether the sweeteners themselves contribute to changes in brain function, why certain groups appear more strongly affected, and whether different sugar alternatives produce different long-term outcomes.

The research was supported by the Brazilian Ministry of Health, the Ministry of Science, Technology, and Innovation, and the National Council for Scientific and Technological Development.

#5697. Strengthening Healthcare Delivery Through Proactive Primary Care

Strengthening Healthcare Delivery Through Proactive Primary Care" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

A stroke can happen without warning. In the months beforehand, however, there may have been a blood pressure reading that needed attention, a prescription that lapsed or a follow-up visit that never got scheduled. Primary care is usually where those signals surface first, and where there is the best chance to act before an emergency.

Much of that work happens between appointments. Care teams review charts ahead of visits, call patients after a hospital discharge and follow up on overdue screenings. Traditional fee-for-service pays for the visit itself but offers little support for the proactive work around it. Value-based care shifts the focus from the volume of services delivered to the quality, outcomes and total cost of care. By aligning financial incentives with prevention, it helps keep patients healthy and out of the hospital while strengthening the long-term financial sustainability of the practice.

For people with traditional Medicare, the Medicare Shared Savings Program (MSSP) enables primary care practices to be paid for that preventive work. MSSP is a permanent, voluntary accountable care program run within traditional Medicare by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS). Physician groups, health systems and community health centers participate by joining an accountable care organization (ACO), which takes responsibility for the quality and total cost of care for its assigned patients.

Clinicians continue to bill Medicare for covered services under fee-for-service, and MSSP adds a layer of value-based savings on top. When proactive primary care lowers the total cost of patients' care against a historical benchmark, often by preventing avoidable hospitalizations and emergency visits, and the ACO meets quality standards, Medicare shares a portion of those savings with the ACO. Because savings stem directly from keeping people healthy, clinical goals and financial rewards finally pull in the same direction. Shared savings are not guaranteed and depend on multiple factors.

The program operates at significant scale. In performance year 2026, 511 ACOs are serving 12.6 million people with traditional Medicare.¹ In performance year 2024, 75% of participating ACOs earned shared savings, and the program produced roughly $2.5 billion in net savings for Medicare.²

Physician-led value-based care puts primary care physicians and practices at the center of care delivery and decision-making. Shared savings give primary care organizations a revenue stream tied to prevention, which they can reinvest in staff, outreach and technology.

An ACO enablement partner can provide the data, care model support and operational infrastructure needed to identify patient needs, coordinate care and manage the ACO's reporting to Medicare, while participating primary care organizations retain control over how they deliver care. Aledade is one such partner. In fact, practices with five or more years with Aledade deliver approximately three times higher savings than the national average for non-Aledade ACOs of similar tenure.3

With that support and the actionable insights and clinical guidance it brings, primary care teams can reach the right patient at the right time, and the results show up as an emergency visit avoided, a stroke prevented or a hospital stay that never happened. For patients, prevention can mean more birthdays, more holidays and more time with the people they love.

Aledade is a physician-led value-based care company and the leading value-based care participant in MSSP.4 Aledade works alongside primary care organizations to put proactive care into practice through true financial alignment. Within its ACOs, savings are generally allocated approximately 50% to Aledade and 50% to its practice partners, with individual practice distributions weighted by quality performance and other contractual terms.⁵ That means Aledade succeeds only when its primary care partners do.

For more than a decade, Aledade has partnered with thousands of primary care organizations through the ACOs it forms and manages, providing data, technology, care model support and operational infrastructure. Together, these capabilities help clinicians identify patient needs earlier, coordinate care and build a sustainable financial model that helps direct more revenue to primary care. When primary care is financially incentivized to keep patients healthy, warning signs can be caught earlier and life-threatening events can be prevented.

1 2026 Medicare Accountable Care Organization Initiatives Participation Highlights, CMS.

2 CMS Proposes Transformational Medicare Reforms to Expand Accountable Care, CMS, July 2026.

3 Aledade analysis of CMS Public Use File of MSSP annual results through 2024; for Aledade data incorporates private CMS data for 2025; weighted average of performance for all data 2015+, incorporates Aledade 2016+ cohorts.

4 Based on internal analysis of data from the 2024 CMS ACO Public Use File.

5 Based on Aledade's standard ACO contractual terms as of January 1, 2026.

#5696. GLP-1 Pill Shows Benefit in Sleep Apnea

— If approved, orforglipron could become the first oral treatment for obstructive sleep apnea

The oral GLP-1 receptor agonist orforglipron (Foundayo) improved sleep-disordered breathing in patients with moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea and overweight or obesity, two phase III trials showed.

For the treatment regimen estimand, mean change of apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) was significantly improved from baseline to week 52 with orforglipron compared with placebo both in patients receiving continuous positive airway pressure (PAP; -17.3 vs -5.3 events/hour, P<0.001) and in patients not receiving PAP (-17.8 vs -4.5 events/hour, P<0.001).

Orforglipron also showed significant improvements in secondary outcomes, including the sleep apnea-specific hypoxic burden, as well as reductions in body weight, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein, and blood pressure, reported Vaishnavi Kundel, MD, of the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in New York City.

"These data support the potential use of orforglipron as a promising oral treatment option for moderate-to-severe OSA [obstructive sleep apnea] in adults with obesity or overweight," Kundel said at the American Heart Association (AHA) annual meeting held in Chicago.

AHA commenter Michael Grandner, PhD, from the University of Arizona in Tucson, said having an oral option to treat obstructive sleep apnea would be "game-changing."

"As a reminder, to treat sleep apnea right now, we have instruments that work really well, but they can be complicated and difficult to use," Grandner said. "Not only is it undertreated, but among those who are treated, use is relatively low. This might help get people toward the treatment that they need."

The results of the ATTAIN-OSA trials were published simultaneously in JAMA.

Orforglipron is a small-molecule, non-peptide oral GLP-1 receptor agonist that has already received FDA approval for weight management.

In an editorial accompanying the publication, Diego Mazzotti, PhD, and Damien Stevens, MD, both of the University of Kansas Medical Center in Kansas City, pointed out that for patients with severe disease, "it is expected that orforglipron will be one component of a broader treatment plan."

They suggested that pragmatic trials comparing and combining orforglipron with PAP, oral appliances, tirzepatide (Mounjaro, Zepbound), or other treatments are needed. "For many years, individuals with OSA had few alternatives when PAP was inadequate," they wrote. "Orforglipron adds an oral option to a growing number of treatments from which clinicians and patients can select and work together to build better individualized care."

AHA discussant for the presentation, Ildiko Lingvay, MD, MPH, of the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center in Dallas, compared the results for orforglipron to those reported for another GLP-1 drug, tirzepatide, which is already approved for obstructive sleep apnea.

She pointed to apparent advantages for tirzepatide over orforglipron in terms of obstructive sleep apnea disease control, with greater improvement in AHI as well as in hypoxic burden, and in safety measures. Cardiovascular risk reduction is also not yet established with orforglipron, while tirzepatide is already FDA-approved for cardiovascular risk reduction in people with diabetes.

"The biggest benefit of orforglipron is really the fact that it comes in a tablet form, for once-daily administration, while tirzepatide requires a cold chain supply and injections," Lingvay noted. "The take-home message is that orforglipron is the first ever oral therapy to have shown improvements in disordered breathing as well as beneficial effects on cardiovascular risk factors, and that includes weight, systolic blood pressure, and inflammatory markers."

The ATTAIN-OSA program included two 52-week, phase III, multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials involving patients on PAP (N=349) or not on PAP (N=363). The studies were carried out at 66 sites in the U.S., Argentina, Brazil, China, the Czech Republic, Germany, Japan, Mexico, and Taiwan.

Adults with moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea and a body mass index of 27 or higher were eligible. Participants were randomly assigned to receive either once-daily orforglipron at the maximum tolerated dose, equivalent to a 9-, 14.5-, or 17.2-mg tablet dose, or placebo.

Gastrointestinal events were the most commonly reported adverse events, occurring in 68% of patients on orforglipron versus 37.4% of those on placebo among the trial participants not on PAP, and in 70.6% of those on orforglipron versus 36.6% of those on placebo in the PAP trial.

#5695. Closing the last mile of value-based care with AI

Closing the last mile of value-based care with AI" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

One of the most challenging parts of value-based care is its timing. Too often, diagnosis gaps or risks arrive late, after an appointment or follow-up, when there is less opportunity to improve care and results.

This is a persistent last-mile challenge in VBC: translating population-level information into action within everyday workflows. Reports, payer portals, and standalone analytics tools may identify important opportunities, but practices are often left on their own to connect those insights to the clinicians and teams responsible for addressing them.

AI can help close that distance. Instead of simply generating more insights, AI combined with clinical and payer data can surface actionable intelligence at the point in time when teams address care gaps, evaluate diagnoses, and monitor VBC performance.

Put VBC insights where clinicians can act on them

Identifying a potential diagnosis gap is only part of the job. A clinician still needs enough information to determine whether the diagnosis is supported by the patient’s record and, if so, document it appropriately. If finding that evidence requires searching through the chart or consulting a separate tool, a useful insight can create additional work before it leads to action.

The stakes are also rising. As scrutiny of risk-adjustment coding increases, practices need confidence that every documented diagnosis is supported by the record. An AI suggestion surfaced without clearly documented rationale can add risk, instead of the opposite.

This raises the standard for AI in diagnosis-gap workflows. Each suggested gap should come paired with clinical evidence that references relevant lab and imaging results, vital signs, and clinical notes, so that clinicians can quickly evaluate recommendations within the visit time.

athenahealth’s Clinically Inferred Diagnosis Gaps was built around this model. It uses generative AI to analyze existing chart information and surface potential gaps related to the CMS-HCC risk-adjustment model, along with supporting evidence, inside the clinician’s existing workflow.

Bring payer insights into the clinical workflow

With visibility across care settings, payers have a unique line of insight into patients’ overall care journeys. This more comprehensive view may reveal potential diagnosis gaps beyond what a clinician encounters during an individual visit. Bringing those payer-supplied gaps into the clinical workflow can give clinicians additional information to consider while the patient is in front of them.

New workflows connect payer insights with point-of-care clinical actionability. athenahealth’s moment of care diagnosis-gap workflow allows payers to flag a potential diagnosis gap prior to an upcoming appointment, allowing clinicians enough time to review during the encounter. If the clinician determines that a diagnosis is appropriate, they can document it through the existing workflow and can even close the loop by sharing information back to the payer about how the gap was addressed.

Find VBC opportunities across your patient population

For true value at scale, organizations need to be able to look beyond individual patient visits and at their broader populations. Quality and population health leaders need to answer practical questions across entire patient populations: Which patients still have an open care gap? How are clinicians performing on specific quality measures? Where should the team focus its attention next? Getting those answers can require configuring reports, combining results, or exporting data for further analysis.

AI tools offer powerful new ways to facilitate a macro view, plumbing data to surface trends, emerging needs, and risk profiles that can help direct strategies. Rather than requiring users to translate each question into a predefined report, Sage™, athenaOne’s AI assistant, gives them another way to investigate VBC performance and zero in on the patients, clinicians, or measures that need a closer look. For independent practices, that can make population-level information more accessible to the people responsible for turning it into action.

Reduce the work between VBC insight and action

The value-based care burden can be heavy for independent practices with thinner teams and fewer resources. Integrated AI-native platforms with smarter insights, payer data, population analytics, and performance reporting can help practices manage the coordinated efforts required to succeed in VBC.

When these stakeholders and systems can communicate, their independent value becomes exponentially greater. When information is spread across separate reports, payer portals, analytics tools, and clinical systems, practice teams may have to find and reconcile data before they can decide what needs attention.

Bringing more of that intelligence into the environment where clinicians and quality teams already work creates a more direct path: Find an opportunity → add relevant context → get the information to someone who can act → understand performance.

That is the larger opportunity for AI-enabled VBC: not simply generating more information, but making useful clinical, payer, and performance insights easier to put to work.

#5694. A surprising vitamin A discovery is changing what scientists know about vision

Scientists at Johns Hopkins University have uncovered a surprising role for a vitamin A derivative in the development of human vision. Their research reveals how this molecule works alongside thyroid hormones to help form the part of the eye responsible for our sharpest sight, challenging a scientific explanation that has stood for roughly 30 years.

The discovery centers on an unexpected transformation that occurs in the developing retina before birth. Certain cells that initially detect blue light appear to change into cells sensitive to red and green light, helping create the specialized arrangement needed for clear central vision.

Published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, the findings could reshape scientists' understanding of how human eyes develop. They may also help advance research into future treatments for macular degeneration, glaucoma, and other conditions that cause vision loss.

"This is a key step toward understanding the inner workings of the center of the retina, a critical part of the eye and the first to fail in people with macular degeneration," said Robert J. Johnston Jr., an associate professor of biology at Johns Hopkins University who led the study. "By better understanding this region and developing organoids that mimic its function, we hope to one day grow and transplant these tissues to restore vision."

How Scientists Recreated the Developing Human Retina

To investigate how human vision forms, Johnston and his colleagues turned to an innovative laboratory technique they have helped develop over the past several years. Instead of relying entirely on animal experiments, they grew miniature versions of human retinal tissue called organoids.

These small clusters of cells, grown from fetal cells, reproduce important features of developing human tissue. By observing the retinal organoids over several months, the scientists could follow changes that would otherwise be extremely difficult to study during pregnancy.

Their attention focused on the foveola, a tiny region at the very center of the retina. The retina is the light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye that converts incoming light into signals the brain can interpret. Within it, the foveola plays an especially important role in detailed central vision, which allows people to read, recognize faces, and distinguish fine details.

Although the foveola occupies only a small fraction of the retina, it is involved in approximately 50% of human visual perception, according to the researchers.

The Surprising Secret Behind Sharp Human Vision

One of the keys to understanding the foveola is a group of specialized light-detecting cells called cones. Unlike rod cells, which are particularly important for seeing in dim light, cones support daytime vision and allow us to perceive color.

Humans have three types of cone cells, each most sensitive to different wavelengths of light. These are commonly described as blue, green, and red cones. By comparing signals from these different cells, the brain can distinguish a remarkably broad range of colors.

However, the cones are not distributed evenly throughout the retina. The foveola contains red and green cones but lacks blue cones, which are found in other retinal regions. This precise arrangement is essential for the exceptionally sharp vision produced by the center of the eye.

For decades, researchers have struggled to explain how this pattern develops. One major obstacle is that commonly studied animals, including mice and fish, do not share the same retinal organization found in humans. That makes it difficult to use traditional animal models to investigate how these specialized cells develop.

The laboratory-grown human retinas offered a new opportunity to solve this longstanding mystery.

Vitamin A and Thyroid Hormones Trigger a Remarkable Change

The researchers discovered evidence that the arrangement of cones in the foveola develops through two coordinated processes. Together, they determine which types of cells form in the central retina and how some of those cells change as development continues.

During weeks 10 through 12 of fetal development, a small number of blue cones are initially present in the foveola. By week 14, however, these cells appear to have transformed into red and green cones.

The team identified two important chemical influences behind this process.

The first involves retinoic acid, a molecule produced from vitamin A. Retinoic acid helps regulate how cells develop and specialize throughout the body. In the developing retina, the breakdown of this molecule limits the formation of blue cones in the central region.

The second influence comes from thyroid hormones, which are best known for regulating metabolism but also have crucial roles in growth and development. In this case, the hormones appear to encourage the remaining blue cones to change into red and green cones.

"First, retinoic acid helps set the pattern. Then, thyroid hormone plays a role in converting the leftover cells," Johnston said. "That's very important because if you have those blue cones in there, you don't see as well."

Importantly, the discovery concerns how vitamin A signaling helps guide eye development before birth. It does not establish that taking vitamin A supplements can improve sharp vision in adults.

A Discovery That Challenges a 30-Year-Old Theory

The results offer a striking alternative to an explanation that has influenced vision research for decades.

Under the longstanding model, blue cones that initially appear in the foveola were thought to move away as the retina developed. Scientists generally assumed that once these cells became a particular type of cone, their identities remained fixed.

The new findings suggest something different. Rather than simply relocating, at least some blue cones may undergo a change in identity, becoming red or green cones as the eye develops.

"The main model in the field from about 30 years ago was that somehow the few blue cones you get in that region just move out of the way, that these cells decide what they're going to be, and they remain this type of cell forever," Johnston said. "We can't really rule that out yet, but our data supports a different model. These cells actually convert over time, which is really surprising."

The researchers have not completely ruled out the possibility that some cells migrate. Nevertheless, their observations support the idea that developing cone cells have more flexibility than previously recognized.

That possibility could fundamentally change how scientists study the formation of human color vision and the development of the retina's most specialized regions.

Could the Discovery Help Scientists Restore Lost Vision?

Beyond explaining how healthy eyes develop, the findings could have important implications for treating diseases that damage the retina.

One particularly promising application involves macular degeneration, a major cause of central vision loss, especially among older adults. The disease damages the macula, the retinal region responsible for detailed central vision, and can severely interfere with reading, driving, and recognizing faces. Although treatments can slow or manage certain forms of the disease, there is currently no cure.

Understanding how the retina creates its specialized light-sensitive cells could eventually help scientists produce healthy replacements in the laboratory.

Johnston's team is now working to improve its retinal organoids so they more closely reproduce the structure and function of the human eye. The long-term goal is to develop precisely controlled populations of photoreceptors, the cells that detect light, for potential transplantation into damaged retinas.

Katarzyna Hussey, a study author and former doctoral student in Johnston's laboratory, believes this approach could open an important new direction for vision restoration. Hussey is now a molecular and cell biologist at CiRC Biosciences, a cell therapy company in Chicago.

"The goal with using this organoid tech is to eventually make an almost made-to-order population of photoreceptors. A big avenue of potential is cell replacement therapy to introduce healthy cells that can reintegrate into the eye and potentially restore that lost vision," said Hussey.

The idea is to introduce healthy cells that could integrate with existing retinal tissue and potentially replace functions lost to disease. Achieving that goal would require researchers to demonstrate that transplanted cells can survive, connect properly with the eye's existing circuitry, and function safely.

Hussey emphasized that the technology remains far from routine clinical use, with extensive development and testing still necessary.

"These are very long-term experiments, and of course we'd need to do optimizations for safety and efficacy studies prior to moving into the clinic. But it's a viable journey."

For now, the discovery provides something fundamental: a clearer explanation of how the human eye develops its remarkable ability to see fine details. By revealing how vitamin A signaling and thyroid hormones help shape the retina, scientists have taken another step toward understanding vision at its earliest stages and potentially finding ways to restore it when disease strikes.

#5692. Agricultural Visionary: Stefan Soloviev's Path to Innovation

Entrepreneur Stefan Soloviev has created an indelible impression in the global agribusiness landscape. Known for his innovative approach and dedication to sustainability, his journey provides essential insights into successful entrepreneurship in this challenging yet rewarding industry.

Breaking Ground: Stefan Soloviev's Foray into Agribusiness

When talking about Stefan Soloviev, one cannot ignore his impressive transition into the agribusiness sector. He recognized the immense potential in this industry, which is evident in his ownership of Crossroads Agriculture, managing more than 70,000 acres of farmland from New Mexico to Colorado1. His entrepreneurial spirit and strategic foresight have enabled him to cultivate success in this multifaceted industry.

#5691. IBM builds on hybrid cloud and governance to advance its enterprise AI operating model

Enterprises are moving beyond AI pilots, putting greater emphasis on governance, production readiness and measurable business outcomes.

Research from Deloitte highlights a significant gap between enterprise AI ambition and execution: 54% of organizations plan to move at least 40% of their AI initiatives into production within six months. Yet only 25% have done so today. IBM is betting on its strengths — mainframe hardware, hybrid computing assets and a legacy of strong governance — to gain a leg up on the rest of the market, according to theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante.

“In our opinion, IBM has found a differentiated path in enterprise AI by productizing workflow-level outcomes across a stack that, while sometimes confusing, customers generally trust,” he said. “Client Zero proof, a workload-first hybrid design, durable platforms reimagined for agents and a pragmatic quantum roadmap create a credible basis for sustained advantage.”

This feature is part of SiliconANGLE Media’s exploration of how enterprise AI has moved beyond the race for model supremacy, with major technology players now focused on enabling governed enterprise AI that delivers trust, reliability and predictable business outcomes. (* Disclosure below.)

IBM already has a substantial book of business around generative AI, with AI-related software sales and consulting engagements totaling more than $12.5 billion as of Q4 2025, up from $9.5 billion the previous quarter.

Through a series of investments, acquisitions and product launches, IBM is gathering assets for an enterprise AI operating model with four pillars: agent orchestration, trusted data, intelligent operations and governance.

Many of these capabilities were rolled out as part of a steady drumbeat of announcements leading up to IBM Think 2026 in May. In February, the company announced a partnership with Deepgram Inc. to integrate voice capabilities into watsonx Orchestrate, its enterprise platform for building, deploying and managing agents. Two months later, it made IBM Bob — an AI-assisted coding tool that helps developers plan, write, test, modernize and deploy code —  globally available.

In May 2026, IBM completed its acquisition of Confluent, the data streaming platform, to enhance watsonx.data. By integrating streaming and real-time data, IBM aims to make watsonx.data the trusted data foundation, providing AI agents with continuously updated context.

At Think 2026, the company repositioned Concert from a point product into an agentic IT operations platform designed to unify observability, optimization, security and automation across hybrid environments. The move positions Concert as the intelligent operations layer of IBM’s broader enterprise AI strategy.

The IBM Sovereign Core platform announced at Think 2026 is designed to address the final pillar: governance. It helps enterprises build and operate AI-ready sovereign environments by embedding governance, compliance and operational control directly into the underlying infrastructure.

June brought more AI-related announcements: IBM joined OpenAI’s Daybreak Cyber Partner Program, which aims to identify AI-driven cybersecurity threats. IBM has partnered with Google Cloud to help IBM consultants design, build and govern enterprise-grade agents on Google Cloud.

All these announcements paint a picture: IBM wants to be the one-stop shop for enterprise AI, and to do so, it is investing significantly in new capabilities while leaning on its reputation for trusted enterprise security and governance, according to theCUBE Research’s John Furrier.

“While others chase frontier models, IBM is betting on something harder: trusted AI in production,” he told theCUBE. “The question coming out of Think is simple — are they becoming the system of record for enterprise AI or just another layer in the stack?”

In a media briefing ahead of Think 2026, IBM Chief Executive Arvind Krishna pointed out that over 70% of all enterprise data remains locked up in on-premises systems. That makes hybrid cloud a critical component of IBM’s enterprise AI operating model, allowing enterprises to use corporate data for AI workloads without abandoning existing infrastructure.

Recent earnings reports appear to reinforce IBM’s bet on hybrid cloud in the AI era. Red Hat Inc., whose OpenShift Kubernetes platform underpins IBM’s hybrid cloud software portfolio, saw revenue increase 13% year over year. Meanwhile, revenue from IBM Z, the company’s mainframe platform, saw revenues grow 51% year over year, underscoring the continued importance of mainframes in IBM’s infrastructure business.

IBM is embedding AI technology directly into IBM Z mainframes to support demanding AI workloads, according to Ric Lewis, senior vice president of the Infrastructure Division at IBM.  This strategy has resonated with clients and led to 20%-30% program-to-program growth for almost a decade. Z mainframes, a key priority for enterprises looking to deploy AI while maintaining control over their data and systems, are also a pillar of IBM’s sovereignty strategy.

“Sovereignty is our home court. We do 70% of the world’s financial transactions,” Lewis told theCUBE. “The most important data that travels around the world is in our Z systems. Those are sovereign systems. They’re on-prem, they’re in environments, they’re in banks, they’re in financial institutions, they’re in insurance. Sovereign is our home court, and we know this space extremely well.”

IBM’s view of sovereignty centers on customer control: keeping critical data and AI workloads in environments customers own and govern, rather than depending entirely on third-party infrastructure. Javier Olaizola, global managing partner for hybrid cloud and data at IBM Consulting, explained that the topic is coming up earlier in client engagements.

“Sovereignty and exposure was coming in on slide 40 in a PowerPoint pitch,” he told theCUBE. “Now it’s coming up front: ‘How much is my exposure?’ That is coming up with a new set of conversations that we are having with clients.”

Sovereign Core is the company’s answer to those questions, according to Sripriya Srinivasan, general manager for Core and ALM software products at IBM. Its goal is to help companies maintain operational consistency even as AI regulations and geopolitics constantly shift. It also helps companies contend with massive AI agent sprawl.

“The proliferation of agents is real in enterprises. Everybody is starting to build agents,” Srinivasan told theCUBE. “How do you, as a [chief information officer], make sure that there’s a level of standardization, consistency, governance, orchestration? All of these are internal fears, not necessarily coming, just based on regulations.”

How does this all translate to real-world results? It’s useful to look back at Krishna’s comments from Think 2026, where he presented IBM’s point of view on what makes a successful enterprise AI strategy.

“The enterprises pulling ahead are not deploying more AI; they’re redesigning how their business operates,” Krishna said during a media briefing.

IBM sets its own example by viewing itself as Client Zero for its enterprise AI strategy, according to James Kavanaugh, senior vice president and chief financial officer of IBM.

“AI is now embedded across our business, from how we deliver services to our software portfolio to the capabilities we are adding to our infrastructure platforms and how we drive our own productivity,” he said.

IBM reports that more than 80,000 of its employees use IBM Bob, with users reporting more than a 45 percent increase in productivity. Additionally, IBM Consulting has deployed more than 4,000 digital workers across 450 active projects, including agents from watsonx, Anthropic PBC and OpenAI Group PBC.

To keep this digital workforce under control, the company relies on a management philosophy that treats AI agents like human workers, an idea that Krishna himself suggested, explained Mohamad Ali, senior vice president and head of IBM Consulting.

“Arvind called me, and we had a conversation about three years ago, and he said, ‘I want you to come over, and I want you to be a consulting business,’” he said in an interview with theCUBE. “‘What is digital labor? It’s a whole bunch of bits of software. I need you to come in, and I need you to build this set of software and do it in a way that it could be managed. You could think of this as HR management … but now you have to HR manage human workers and digital workers.’”

IBM customers are also putting elements of the enterprise AI operating model into practice. Global bank BNP Paribas SA has nearly 1,000 AI use cases underway across its operations, using a group-level framework with governance distributed across business units and functions.

“The strategy is to use AI, not to become AI — to use AI to better serve our customers and to give more value to them,” Jean-Michel Garcia, group chief technology officer at BNP Paribas, told theCUBE. “But also internally, for employees, to give them more capabilities to focus on the right set of tasks and to make them more efficient and more focused on what they do.”

(* Disclosure: TheCUBE is a paid media partner for the IBM Think event. Neither IBM, the sponsor of theCUBE’s event coverage, nor other sponsors have editorial control over content on theCUBE or SiliconANGLE.)

#5690. From Fragmentation to Integration: A New Model for Specialty Care

From Fragmentation to Integration: A New Model for Specialty Care" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Health systems are navigating growing demands with increasingly limited resources. As costs rise and teams are stretched, technology has become essential to helping people work smarter. But technology alone isn’t the answer. Many health systems and specialty care teams are discovering that more tools don’t always mean a more efficient process or better patient outcomes.

Approximately 25% of healthcare spending in the U.S. goes toward administrative expenses. At the same time, 60% of hospitals and health systems use more than 50 software solutions for operations. Yet more technology hasn’t meant less complexity. Care teams still navigate disconnected tools, siloed data, fragmented workflows, and manual handoffs. The opportunity isn’t to add more technology; it’s to make everything work better together.

Health systems want to better manage the specialty patient journey, but administrative burdens get in the way of more coordinated care. What they need is an integrated approach – one that improves patient experiences and outcomes by connecting workflows through technology and adding dedicated human expertise to serve as an extension of existing care teams.

When specialty care teams spend more time navigating processes and technology than focusing on patients, trust erodes, costs rise, and turnover climbs. It also limits teams’ ability to apply the clinical expertise and personalized attention that complex specialty care requires. This friction shows up in three core areas:

The rapid adoption of specialized software and standalone tools for tasks such as scheduling, patient intake, and remote monitoring fragments care delivery. Teams constantly toggle between platforms, manually piecing together a single patient’s record. This can contribute to cognitive overload among care teams, a factor in burnout, and it diverts valuable time and attention from clinical decision-making and personalized patient support that require human expertise.

Point solutions may solve individual challenges, but they often operate in isolation. When systems don’t fully connect, patient information becomes fragmented across applications, leaving specialty care teams without visibility into the full context of a patient’s broader care journey. This can increase the risk of redundant testing, duplicated work, and inaccurate reporting, while making it harder for clinicians to identify when patients may need additional interventions.

The care journey includes multiple critical transitions, from cross-departmental referrals to prescription routing to external coordination. Despite healthcare’s digital process, these transitions still rely too frequently on faxes, phone calls, and manual spreadsheets. The added administrative burden makes it harder for care teams to coordinate timely interventions and provide consistent, personalized support. Without an integrated model that connects the entire care journey, referrals or post-procedure care plans can fall through the cracks.

Complexity comes at a cost: time teams could be spending on patient care. According to AMA research, for every hour physicians spend with patients, they spend nearly two more on EHR and desk work.

For specialty care teams, disconnected technology and fragmented workflows can make it even harder to see the full picture of a patient’s care. Patients with multiple chronic conditions, for example, often see several specialists. When any one of them lacks complete visibility into the patient’s full treatment plan, specialty performance breaks down. The risk of prescribing therapies that shouldn't be combined rises, potentially compromising patient safety and delaying therapy.

Solving today’s specialty care challenges requires more than another point solution. It requires a connected operating model that brings workflows, information and expertise together, giving care teams the visibility and support they need to act with greater confidence and keep patients moving forward.

Shields Health Solutions’ integrated care model combines technology, data, and clinical expertise to reduce administrative burden, streamline care coordination, and provide specialty care teams with more time to focus on patients. Rather than relying on technology alone, Shields’ clinical pharmacists and liaisons work as an extension of specialty care teams. They translate insights into action, resolving barriers to therapy, coordinating care, and supporting patients throughout treatment.

That combination of human expertise and connected technology delivers measurable results. With average time to therapy in under 48 hours compared with the seven-to-10-day industry average, Shields’ integrated care model drives connected performance, alleviating operational strain on care teams while improving access to therapy, better patient outcomes, and long-term growth.

#5689. Bioengineered Liver System Passes Safety Test in Phase I Trial

— The miroliverELAP also showed signs of efficacy in patients with syndromes of liver failure

A single-use bioengineered liver paired with an extracorporeal blood circuit that replicates key functions of a human liver was shown to be safe among patients with syndromes of liver failure in a small phase I trial.

There were no serious or unexpected adverse events (AEs) related to the miroliverELAP system, while every patient was still alive after the scheduled 48 hours of treatment, reported Christopher J. Danford, MD, of Intermountain Health in Salt Lake City, at the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases annual meeting in Denver.

In addition, the system demonstrated signs of efficacy, as there was an improvement in encephalopathy and reductions in vasopressor requirements during the course of treatment.

While none of the patients in the study were transplant candidates, "many of them would have been potentially transplantable by the end of treatment, and based on those results, we're moving forward with our phase II and III clinical trial," Danford noted.

Syndromes of liver failure -- fulminant hepatic failure, acute alcoholic hepatitis (AAH), and acute-on-chronic liver failure (ACLF) -- are devastating conditions for which there's no good treatment other than liver transplant. Due to the lack of transplantable livers and the rapid onset of acute liver failure, a significant number of patients die before getting access to a liver transplant.

"The hope is that an external bioengineered liver may provide some support that either bridges the patient to recovery or transplant," Danford said. "However, there are no previous studies in humans involving a bioengineered liver."

The FDA granted a Regenerative Medicine Advanced Therapy designation to the miroliverELAP system for the treatment of acute liver failure in April. As described by its maker in a press release, the bioengineered liver is manufactured "by seeding a decellularized porcine liver scaffold with allogeneic human endothelial cells and human liver cells isolated from donated human livers." These donated livers are not considered suitable for transplantation and are provided by organ procurement organizations.

This study included seven critically ill patients who initiated therapy, five of whom completed the planned therapy (ranging in age from 27 to 43).

The primary etiology was AAH in four patients, and ACLF in the fifth, with a mean Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) score of 36.

Inclusion criteria included a MELD score ≥20, an International Normalized Ratio (INR) ≥2.0, and a West Haven hepatic encephalopathy (HE) grade of 1-3, while patients were excluded if eligible for transplantation.

Primary endpoints were serious AEs attributable to the system, and survival for the duration of the therapy. Secondary endpoints included 21-day post-treatment survival.

Three of the five patients who completed therapy were alive 21 days post-treatment.

There were a total of 42 AEs, with 17 occurring during treatment (11 possibly or probably related to treatment). System-related AEs among the full seven patients included grade 2-3 thrombocytopenia (four patients), anemia (three patients), bleeding (two patients), hypotension (two patients), and worsening lactic acidosis (one patient).

Twenty-five AEs occurred after therapy, one of which, a gastrointestinal bleed, was deemed possibly related to treatment. There were six serious AEs after therapy, including five deaths related to liver disease progression.

While this was primarily a safety study, "there were some promising [efficacy] signs," Danford noted.

Of the five patients who completed treatment, four experienced improvement in encephalopathy, with improvement sustained 48 hours post-treatment. In addition, while three of the five patients were on significant vasopressor therapy at baseline, all five were either off vasopressors or had their requirements reduced by 75% at the completion of the trial.
